## [Mechanistic Study Dissects How Hierarchical Reasoning Models Reason](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22197) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22197) presents a mechanistic analysis of the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) on Sudoku, Maze, and ARC-AGI-2, comparing it against Transformer baselines with and without recurrent modules and applying causal interventions on recurrent states. The study finds that recurrent models outperform one-pass baselines, that single-state recurrent Transformers are comparable to HRM, and that the causal roles of high- and low-level states vary by task checkpoint and inference stage. This work matters because it challenges the assumption that HRM's hierarchical two-level architecture is the source of its reasoning power, suggesting a simpler single-state recurrent design may suffice. It also shows that standard interpretability tools like linear probes and sparse autoencoders fail to find a compact, causally important feature set in latent recursive reasoning models, pointing to a need for new interpretability techniques. Linear probes can decode selected task variables from HRM's recurrent states, but ablating probe directions produces effects comparable to random controls; SAE ablations cause larger behavioral changes, yet top-ranked SAE features show no stable advantage over size-matched random subsets at larger ablation sizes or across tasks. The authors conclude HRM essentially performs constraint-aware iterative refinement on a puzzle-specific solution state, without relying on a compact, causally important feature set.

## [PII-TRACE Benchmark Exposes Gaps in Multi-Turn PII Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22200) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced PII-TRACE, the first benchmark for context-aware PII detection in multi-turn LLM conversations, comprising 13,148 synthetic dialogues in 13 languages with character-level spans and identifier clusters. Evaluating eleven baselines including frontier LLMs, they found no detector achieves full entity-level coverage without substantial false positives on PII-free conversations, and single-pass reading loses a third of gold characters on long dialogues; they also released PII-Tracer, a 0.6B-parameter detector trained with conversation-level supervision that attains the highest entity-level coverage. This work highlights a critical unsolved problem in privacy-preserving AI: existing PII detectors, including frontier LLMs, fail to reliably cover every mention of recurring identifiers across turns, which could lead to privacy leaks in logged conversations. The benchmark and compact detector provide a foundation for improving PII masking in agentic systems and multi-turn assistants, affecting AI providers, privacy engineers, and compliance teams. PII-TRACE contains 13,148 synthetic multi-turn dialogues in 13 languages with character-level spans and identifier clusters, and across eleven baselines no detector achieves full entity-level coverage without substantial false positives on PII-free conversations. PII-Tracer, a compact 0.6B-parameter model trained with conversation-level supervision, attains the highest entity-level coverage of any system evaluated and also performs strongly on standard single-record benchmarks.

Using feedback from a surrogate detector based on the PAN 2025 mdok system, full fine-tuning with a small KL regularization penalty achieves 98.5% surrogate evasion, compared to just 1.5% for the base model. This work demonstrates that reinforcement learning can dramatically undermine current AI-text detectors, raising serious concerns for academic integrity, content moderation, and misinformation detection. It also shows that optimizing against a single surrogate detector only partially transfers to unseen classifiers, motivating more robust multi-detector evaluation protocols. Linguistic analysis reveals that successful evasion correlates with shorter, simpler, and less lexically diverse outputs, suggesting high detector evasion does not necessarily mean more human-like writing. In the official Voight-Kampff competition, the team's submissions ranked sixth and seventh, and LoRA-based adaptation proved substantially less effective under regularization than full fine-tuning.

## [Eurostat Benchmark Tests Whether Coding Agents Can Reproduce Official Statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22222) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22222) presents a controlled Eurostat benchmark of 30 natural-language tasks spanning seven domains, seven datasets and four difficulty tiers, run under four conditions (task only, task plus frozen metadata card, metadata plus a sanitized execution-feedback repair loop, and metadata plus the same retry budget with no diagnostics). Using Claude Sonnet 5 via the Anthropic Messages API across three replicates, the study produced 360 task-runs and found that a companion experiment with an under-specified output contract understated condition C by 23.4 points. The result challenges the common assumption that executable code equals correct analysis, showing that successful execution alone does not guarantee valid official-statistics results. This matters for researchers and practitioners building LLM-based data-analysis agents, because it suggests reliable statistical coding agents need semantic validation against frozen specifications, a fully specified output contract, and a retry budget rather than execution diagnostics. Exact correctness in the benchmark required successful execution plus the correct dataset, filters, output shape, values and unit, making the evaluation stricter than mere runnability. The 23.4-point gap caused by an under-specified output contract shows that evaluator and contract design can dominate measured agent error, and the study is limited to one model (Claude Sonnet 5) and one statistical domain (Eurostat).

## [Net Utility: Budget-Aware LoRA Merging Beats Uniform Rank Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22237) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22237) introduces Net Utility, a data-free metric for selecting how many singular directions each task LoRA should contribute when merging adapters. It decomposes each task LoRA via SVD, scores every singular direction by its task utility minus interference with other tasks, and globally pools the top-scoring directions under a total rank budget. Applied on top of five merging methods across three merging spaces, it yields average gains of +2.1% on vision tasks and +2.2% on language tasks over uniform-budget baselines. Merging LoRA adapters is a practical way to serve many fine-tuned tasks from a single model without swapping weights at inference time, but existing methods assume every layer and every task deserves the same rank budget. Showing that this uniform assumption is a major source of the gap between merged and per-task LoRAs gives the efficient-inference and ML-systems community a concrete, data-free lever for closing that gap. The method is data-free, requiring only the LoRA weights themselves rather than calibration data, and rank selection is framed as an NP-hard problem that Net Utility solves greedily via global pooling under a total-direction constraint. The evaluation covers five merging methods and three merging spaces across vision and language task sets, with reported average improvements of +2.1% and +2.2% respectively.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: LoRA (low-rank adaptation) fine-tunes a large model by adding small low-rank matrices instead of updating all weights, making task-specific customization cheap. When many such adapters exist, merging them into one set of weights avoids loading and swapping separate adapters at inference, but merged models typically underperform the individual task adapters. SVD (singular value decomposition) factorizes a matrix into rotation, scaling, and rotation components, and here it is used to break each LoRA into individual singular directions that can be scored and selectively kept.

## [Chess Study Tests Whether LLM Explanations Reflect Real Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22245) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22245) tests the faithfulness of LLM explanations for chess moves across 200 Lichess endgame puzzles, using move recoverability, decoder-side controls, and token-level scoring of legal candidate moves. It finds that unmasked explanations make generated moves easy to recover, but this advantage drops sharply once explicit move hints are removed, and that random but plausible explanations from other puzzles actually reduce the probability of the correct move. The results suggest that linguistic plausibility, consistency with a generated action, and solution correctness are distinct properties, which challenges the common assumption that fluent LLM explanations are evidence of faithful reasoning. This matters for AI interpretability and evaluation, since users and researchers may over-trust explanations that merely narrate a coherent story rather than reveal the actual decision process. Under strict masking, explanations provide only small and decoder-dependent gains over the board state alone, and recognizable endgame motifs can make generated moves easier to recover without reliably improving move correctness. The study also notes that irrelevant reasoning text is not simply ignored, since plausible explanations from other puzzles measurably shift move preferences.

## [CHART: A Harness-Rotation Curriculum for Robust Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22247) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces CHART (Curriculum HArness Rotation Training), a rotating curriculum that trains search agents to maintain parallel search behavior across different harnesses instead of overfitting to a single one. Starting from the same harness pool, CHART makes the model learn parallel search on all harnesses, whereas static harness augmentation succeeds on at most half of them. Post-trained search agents are fragile to harness updates such as a rewritten system prompt, and this work shows a practical training recipe that makes learned behaviors survive those changes. It matters for anyone deploying LLM agents in production, where harnesses are frequently updated, and it also improves transfer to new QA tasks and search environments. The core insight is that GRPO learns from the reward gap between parallel and serial rollouts of the same question: a small harness pool saturates that gap early, while a large pool dilutes the per-harness signal too thinly. CHART periodically graduates harnesses whose expected behavior is learned and replaces them with still-learnable ones, achieving parallelization on 89% of held-out turns versus at most 5% for static pools, and improving pass@1 by 5.6pp over the best static pool on a new QA task.

**Background**: A harness is the control layer around an LLM agent that decides when the model is called, what prompt and context it receives, which tools it can use, and how the workflow proceeds. Search agents are typically trained under a single harness, but in real deployments the harness is frequently updated, which can break learned behaviors. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm that estimates advantages by normalizing rewards within groups of candidate rollouts, without needing a value critic. Parallel search, in which an agent issues multiple search requests at once rather than one at a time, is a popular strategy for improving both search efficiency and answer quality.

## [Adaptive Teacher Continuations Improve On-Policy Distillation Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22254) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper identifies Teacher Uncertainty Contraction (TUC), a systematic phenomenon in which a teacher model's predictive uncertainty decreases as it continues generating from a student-generated prefix, and proposes Adaptive-Continuations On-Policy Distillation (AC-OPD) to exploit this effect. AC-OPD augments informative states along student rollouts with teacher continuations and adaptively selects their effective supervision horizons, consistently outperforming standard on-policy distillation on mathematical reasoning and code generation across model scales. On-policy distillation is a key technique for transferring knowledge between language models, and unreliable teacher supervision on low-quality student prefixes has been a persistent obstacle to its effectiveness. By providing a principled variance-bias framework for choosing how far a teacher should continue, this work could make distillation more reliable and improve model compression and student training pipelines for the AI/ML community. The paper theoretically characterizes the trade-off through a variance-bias decomposition of teacher-branch gradients: uncertainty contraction reduces variance while teacher-student path divergence increases bias, thereby favoring a finite continuation length rather than an arbitrarily long one. Controlled-continuations and matched-budget analyses validate the adaptive design, and the code is promised to be publicly released upon publication.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a smaller student language model using dense token-level supervision from a larger teacher along trajectories the student itself generates, rather than only on fixed teacher-generated data. A known weakness is that when the student's prefix is incomplete or low-quality, the teacher's next-token predictions conditioned on that prefix can be unreliable. The bias-variance trade-off is a classical statistical concept describing how model error decomposes into systematic bias and variance, and it has recently been applied to analyze knowledge distillation stability.

## [H²V-M Validates VLM and VLA Robustness Over Continuous Perturbation Regions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22293) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces H²V-M, a margin-aware convergence rule built on the H²V validation framework, and uses it to perform the first robustness validation of six VLMs (from the Gemma, InternVL, LLaVA, and Qwen families) and five VLAs (from the GR00T, OpenVLA, and π families) over entire continuous regions of photometric and geometric image perturbation, including brightness shifts, camera rotations, and their composition. H²V-M outperforms the original H²V by an order of magnitude in model queries and finds counterexamples faster than random sampling while providing soundness guarantees, making validation affordable at the 32B parameter scale. Existing robustness benchmarks for VLMs and VLAs only sample perturbations, so they cannot guarantee the absence of failures in untested regions; this work provides formal, region-level soundness guarantees instead. The findings — that robustness depends mostly on perturbation type rather than model, that VLMs tolerate large camera rotations better than VLAs, and that VLA actions can change under perturbations as small as ±1° — have direct implications for the safety and reliability of deployed vision-language and robotic systems. The validation covers photometric perturbations (brightness shifts), geometric perturbations (camera rotations), and their composition, and the authors report that robustness depends more on model family than on model size. A key caveat for practitioners is that for VLAs, even perturbations as small as ±1° can change the commanded action in many cases, and the margin-aware convergence rule is what makes the approach tractable at the 32B parameter scale.

## [Linear Interpolation Proven Optimal for Event Stream Temporal Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22295) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proves a fundamental robustness-resolution tradeoff in temporal quantization of event streams, showing that hard temporal binning is discontinuous and that linear two-bin interpolation is the unique optimal continuous encoder within a class of nonnegative, mass-preserving, resolution-faithful encoders. Experiments on SHD, N-MNIST, and DVS128 Gesture show linear interpolation reduces mean representation drift by 47-72% while keeping clean accuracy nearly unchanged, with zero prediction flips on DVS Gesture across all tested budgets and three seeds. This work provides rigorous theoretical grounding for a preprocessing step widely used in neuromorphic computing and event-based vision, where asynchronous timestamps must be discretized before learning. By identifying linear interpolation as the provably optimal encoder, it offers a simple, low-cost fix that improves representation stability without sacrificing accuracy, potentially benefiting spiking neural networks and event-driven perception pipelines. The paper defines a class of nonnegative, mass-preserving, resolution-faithful continuous encoders and proves every encoder in this class has global L1 sensitivity at least 2/Delta, where Delta is bin width; linear two-bin interpolation attains this limit and is unique due to local support and first-moment preservation. On SHD, measured drift follows 1/Delta with R^2 = 0.992, and on DVS Gesture it produces zero prediction flips across all tested budgets and three seeds.

A new arXiv paper introduces AuthEval, a logging and evaluation framework that records both the AI-proposed action and the locally selected action in medical vision-language assistants, scoring each under declared local criteria to quantify an 'authority gap.' On the ISIC 2019 skin lesion dataset using MedGemma with simulated local review, two constraint regimes with similar proposal-change rates produced an optimistic gap of +0.744 simulator units under capacity constraints but no detectable gap under safety constraints. The authority gap is defined as the product of the proposal-change rate and the mean score change on changed cases, meaning the change rate alone determines neither its magnitude nor its sign. ## [Governance-Aware LLM Agentic Digital Twin for Grid Control Rooms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22476) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces a governance-aware agentic digital twin for transmission system operator control rooms in which the LLM only selects and parameterizes whitelisted analysis tools, and every proposed action passes through a non-bypassable governance layer enforcing four rules: only whitelisted tools execute, no run exceeds its step budget, no side-effecting action runs without explicit operator approval, and every number is rendered by the layer from backend results with its unit, variable, and time. On a released 118-task benchmark using a digital twin of the Greek transmission network, tool selection reached 96.5% and task success 93.7% across 590 runs, with all four rules holding without exception; a separate 1416-run study across four LLMs also held every rule with an approximate 95% lower bound of 99.8%. The work directly addresses the core obstacles to deploying LLM agents in safety-critical infrastructure: hallucinations, uncontrolled tool use, and weak traceability. It offers a reusable design pattern for trustworthy LLM agents in high-stakes environments, showing that strict governance can be enforced at low cost (12–16 ms per request) while preserving high task success. The governance layer is validated on a persistent audit trail for every run, and the benchmark includes analytics, simulation, multi-step workflows, and twelve families of adversarial inputs. Ablation shows that removing the layer causes the same model to execute all 45 approval-requiring runs without authorization and leaves only 39.2% of answers with backend-supported numbers, while enforcement costs only 12 to 16 milliseconds per request.

## [Paper Proposes Weight Operators to Fix Backprop's Weight Entanglement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22554) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22554) identifies a limitation of backpropagation it calls "weight entanglement" — the inability to isolate or reuse functional components because overlapping tasks share parameter sets — and proposes "weight operators," parameterized modules that can be composed at inference time to form the function each sample requires. The authors present Vector Networks (VNs) as one implementation, in which operator selection is coupled to local error-driven updates within each layer, and learning proceeds in two stages: first inferring the required operator composition, then updating only the selected operators' parameters. If functional components could remain tied to identifiable parameter sets, models could reuse and recombine learned functions while adapting only the parts that need to change, potentially improving modularity, continual learning, and parameter efficiency in deep networks. This offers a fresh conceptual angle on a core limitation of backpropagation, though its practical impact depends on the paper's experimental validation. The paper frames the problem against modern architectures that dynamically select which parts of a network process each sample — nonlinearities gating units, attention selecting interactions, and Mixture-of-Experts routing inputs to modules — but argues such selection does not guarantee that the same functional component stays linked to an identifiable parameter set across samples. It proposes "functional parameter identifiability" as a possible organizing principle, and reports that learned operators can be reused in combinations absent from training while updates remain restricted to the selected parameter sets.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Backpropagation is the algorithm that trains modern deep networks by propagating errors backward through layers to update weights end-to-end, but it does not specify how parameters should be organized for reuse. Mixture-of-Experts architectures route each input to a subset of modules, and attention mechanisms select which interactions matter, yet these routing choices are typically made per sample rather than guaranteeing stable parameter-function links. Vector Networks are a neural architecture that represents inputs as sets of vectors and applies operations to them, which the authors use here to couple operator selection with local error-driven updates.

## [Invariance-Weighted Distillation Boosts Student LLM OOD Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22566) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.22566) proposes Invariance-Weighted Distillation (IWD), a framework that dynamically reweights distillation samples based on an estimate of the teacher's causal reliance, derived from prediction invariance across multiple synthetic environments. Experiments on four NLP benchmarks (MNLI, SQuAD-v2, CoNLL-2003 NER, SST-2) with DeBERTa-v3 and Qwen-2.5 show IWD achieves the best accuracy in 15 of 16 OOD settings, improving average OOD performance over standard KD by 4.34 points on NLI and 14.94 points on QA. Knowledge distillation is widely used to compress large teacher LLMs into lightweight students, but distilled students often degrade sharply under distribution shift, which limits their reliability in real-world deployment. By explicitly targeting spurious correlations and teacher reliability, IWD offers a theoretically grounded path toward more robust compressed models, which matters for anyone deploying small models in safety- or domain-sensitive applications. IWD perturbs spurious cues while preserving core semantics, assigning higher distillation weights to samples whose teacher predictions remain invariant across synthetic environments, and the authors theoretically show it reduces the student's Spurious-to-Causal (S2C) gradient ratio relative to uniformly weighted KD. The method maintains competitive in-distribution performance, though results are limited to four NLP benchmarks and two model families, and the paper is a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model's outputs, typically by minimizing a loss over a fixed dataset. Out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness refers to a model's ability to maintain performance when test data differs from the training distribution, a well-known weakness of NLP models. Spurious correlations are dataset-specific shortcuts (e.g., a token that happens to correlate with a label) that models may learn instead of genuine causal features, and causal inference methods aim to distinguish the two by testing whether predictions remain stable under interventions or environment changes.

## [MCP SDKs Fall Short of Enterprise Zero-Trust, Paper Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22573) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22573) presents a systematic gap analysis of six official Model Context Protocol SDKs—Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C#, and Swift—identifying three structural shortcomings: credential extraction bound to a single Authorization header, missing pre-authentication tool discovery, and no fine-grained per-tool authorization. The authors close these gaps with composable FastMCP extensions, including cross-header credential normalization, cached token verification across heterogeneous IdPs, an unauthenticated metadata endpoint, and permission-filtered tool visibility tied to invocation enforcement via a single declarative annotation. As LLM agents increasingly translate attacker-controllable natural-language context into privileged tool calls, weak authorization in MCP SDKs becomes a direct enterprise security risk, especially for prompt-injection attacks. These findings give security and platform engineers concrete, actionable guidance for deploying MCP in zero-trust environments without modifying the protocol or SDK internals. The paper highlights a dual-persona problem where one MCP server must serve human users via corporate SSO and automated agents via service-account credentials on a different header, which single-header extraction complicates without custom middleware. In experiments across four frontier LLMs over 2160 attempts, an in-body-check-only server still exposed forbidden tools in 152/720 cases (21.1%), while permission-aware visibility reduced this to 0/720; visibility-only filtering remained bypassable by scripted clients, and models referenced hidden tools by name in up to 94% of settings when inferable from the prompt.

## [HIGenNTO Generates Humanoid Interaction Motions via Noise-Space Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22611) ⭐️ 7.0/10

HIGenNTO synthesizes humanoid-scene interaction motion references by optimizing the initial noise of a pretrained text-conditioned motion model under sparse spatiotemporal and scene constraints, rather than relying on motion capture or retargeting. The authors deploy the resulting motions on a Unitree G1 humanoid across four contact-rich tasks, and show that a coding agent can author task specifications that compile into prompt, constraint, and scene programs. Reliable contact-rich interaction references are a major bottleneck for humanoid skill learning, since motion capture degrades under occlusion and close contact while retargeting introduces contact and geometric inconsistencies. By generating physically executable motions directly from high-level task descriptions, HIGenNTO points toward a scalable pipeline for training humanoid visuomotor policies without expensive human demonstrations. The same optimization formulation simultaneously satisfies desired contacts, avoids collisions, and maintains stable support while preserving the prior model's realism and temporal coherence, and it can compose long-horizon behaviors stage-wise. The generated motions train depth-conditioned visuomotor policies that operate solely from onboard sensing, and the coding agent authored three of the eight evaluated tasks plus four further behaviors.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Text-conditioned motion diffusion models are generative frameworks that use an iterative denoising process guided by natural language to synthesize diverse 3D human motions, and they are typically trained on large motion datasets. Humanoid motion retargeting is the standard alternative for obtaining robot references, in which human motion data is mapped onto a humanoid embodiment and then imitated by reinforcement learning policies. HIGenNTO instead treats the initial noise of such a pretrained model as the optimization variable, steering generation toward scene-constrained, contact-rich interactions.

## [Paper Proposes Five Assurance Properties for Autonomous Penetration-Testing Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22664) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.22664) defines a framework of five assurance properties for autonomous penetration-testing harnesses: evidence grounding, non-destructive claim reduction, computed severity, enforced authorization, and tamper-evident accountability. The authors position PentestGPT, Cochise, MAPTA, and PentestJudge within the framework, then test the open-source NeuroSploit harness at a pinned commit, finding a real authorization enforcement gap and scoring two properties as partial. Current LLM penetration-testing research is evaluated almost entirely by capability metrics such as capturing a flag, which says nothing about whether findings are true, whether the agent stayed in scope, or whether an operator can audit its actions. This framework shifts the focus toward the safety and auditability properties that determine whether autonomous agents can be trusted in authorized security engagements. Each of the five assurance properties comes with a formal model and an explicit acceptance test, drawing on prior work in capability-based security, tamper-evident logging, and software provenance. The authors emphasize that this is an initial existence argument that the properties are realizable together, not a comparative performance result, and they specify a multi-target, ablation, and adversarial evaluation protocol needed to turn the framework obligations into measurements.

**Background**: LLM agents for penetration testing are increasingly studied, with systems like PentestGPT and multi-agent architectures such as PentAGI automating parts of security assessments. Capability-based security is a long-standing model in which unforgeable tokens grant specific access rights, while tamper-evident audit trails provide sealed chronological records of autonomous system actions. The paper argues that assurance properties belong to the harness — the runtime wrapping the model — rather than the model itself, and can therefore be enforced in code.

## [Vision2CAD Uses VLM Reasoning to Improve Parametric CAD Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22688) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Vision2CAD, a visual agent harness that combines vision-language model (VLM) reasoning with deterministic CAD kernel operations to enable explicit geometry referencing and localization in parametric CAD modeling. They also released the Geometry Explicit Reference Dataset (GERD), and reported mIoU improvements of 11.1% on GERD-EVL and 5.6% on a DeepCAD test subset, with Chamfer distance reductions of 17.3% and 41.8% respectively. This work addresses a core bottleneck in AI-driven CAD generation: reliably selecting and constraining geometric references so that generated models preserve stable parametric dependencies. If validated, such VLM-plus-kernel approaches could make automated design tools more editable and manufacturable, benefiting CAD researchers and engineering software developers. Vision2CAD uses an ID-based interface for explicit geometry selection, a local-coordinate bridge that converts view coordinates into sketch coordinates, and projected-edge localization for external sketch constraints. Ablation studies and parameter-editing experiments were used to demonstrate that parametric dependencies are preserved within the supported modeling operations and constraint types.

## [LLaDA-PRM: Bidirectional Step-Level Reasoning Evaluator Beats Larger Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22700) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced LLaDA-PRM, an 8B bidirectional step-level reasoning evaluator that achieves 88.8 step-level F1 on MR-MATH-invalid and 83.8 on the out-of-distribution MR-GSM8K original-question subset, outperforming the 34B ReasonEval-Llemma by 11.3 and 10.3 F1 points respectively. The work was validated through a controlled 54-run comparison of causal and bidirectional LLaDA evaluators at 1B–3B scale, changing only the self-attention mask. This shows that bidirectional attention can substantially improve step-level reasoning evaluation, allowing a much smaller 8B model to beat a 34B autoregressive baseline. It could shift how process reward models are built and used for training-data selection and online reasoning verification. LLaDA-PRM remains effective when evaluating incomplete reasoning traces in online settings, outperforming the strongest baselines by a large margin on both benchmarks, and it also serves as an effective training-data selection signal that improves Mistral-7B performance on MATH-500. The core finding is that bidirectional attention lets each step representation incorporate downstream consequences, which causal attention cannot do.

**Background**: Process reward models (PRMs) score each intermediate reasoning step rather than only the final answer, helping reveal logical errors that final-answer scoring misses. Most existing step-level evaluators are built on autoregressive language models, whose causal attention restricts each step representation to the problem, previous steps, and the current step. LLaDA is a diffusion language model that uses bidirectional attention, allowing a step to be evaluated with knowledge of what comes after it.

MATE introduces a lightweight, policy-conditioned auditor that encodes both agent trajectories and natural-language security policies to detect and explain violations. As foundation-model-powered mobile agents automate complex multi-step workflows on real devices, their trajectories can violate app-specific security policies, and existing defenses based on LLM prompting or rigid rules cannot handle fine-grained, natural-language policies. MATE shows that practical, editable-policy auditing for heterogeneous mobile agents is feasible, which could improve safety and trust for both users and app developers. Treating policies as editable text rather than fixed model parameters allows MATE to handle user-defined and evolving requirements without retraining. The benchmark MATEBench includes two synthetic subsets and one real-world subset of manually collected trajectories, and models trained with synthesis-driven trajectory learning also retain strong performance on external safety benchmarks.

## [Netflix's Counterfactual Framework Improves Recommender Observability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22747) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Netflix researchers published arXiv:2609.22747, introducing a counterfactual observability framework that treats recommender-system observability as a counterfactual measurement problem. The framework estimates what the recommender would have done, and what engagement would have followed, in the absence of a specific content item or model decision, and was validated through several production deployments across multiple Netflix recommender systems. Raw engagement signals such as views and clicks conflate content quality, model behavior, presentation bias, and audience reach, making it hard for content creators and model developers to attribute outcomes to the right cause. This framework offers a principled way to disentangle these factors at Netflix scale, with implications for how recommender systems across the industry are evaluated and improved. The paper articulates three stakeholder-centered observability principles for content creators and model developers, and proposes measurement methodologies covering bias reduction, relativity, and incrementality. These methodologies are applicable to both single-stage and cascading recommender systems, serving both audiences from a single measurement foundation.

## [SelfOp: Textual Gradient Descent for Self-Improving Security Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22792) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SelfOp is a new algorithm that automatically improves a frozen LLM security agent's task context — its instructions, skills, and reference documents — without changing model weights or the execution harness. It casts context optimization as chain-rule-inspired textual gradient descent, propagating error signals backward from a single instance's outcome through the evaluator, the agent's trajectory, and the context artifacts, then accumulating and committing updates only under cross-instance consensus. On the CyberGym vulnerability reproduction benchmark, fewer than 200 training examples yielded a 17-point gain for GPT-5.4-mini (with Codex), surpassing the frontier GPT-5.4 baseline by 6 points, and an 18.5-point gain for GPT-5.4 itself. Security tasks rarely provide computable rewards or expert demonstrations, so improving LLM agents has largely meant costly manual prompt tuning or trial-and-error loops; SelfOp offers an automated, weight-free path to self-improvement. Because the optimized skills transfer across models, the approach suggests that context-level optimization can capture generalizable task knowledge rather than model-specific quirks, which could change how security agents are built and maintained. SelfOp includes a convergence detector that monitors the gradient signal itself and stops once the context has absorbed the generalizable information in the training data, avoiding the need for held-out validation data. The method operates only on context artifacts and leaves both the execution harness and model weights untouched, and it is evaluated on CyberGym, a benchmark of real-world vulnerability reproduction tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents are increasingly used for security work such as vulnerability discovery, exploit reproduction, and patch generation, but improving them at the model level requires expert demonstrations or computable rewards that security tasks rarely offer. Textual gradient descent is an optimization technique that refines discrete text such as prompts using LLM-generated critique instead of numerical gradients. An agent harness is the scaffolding — prompts, control flow, tooling, memory, and context management — that turns a frozen language model into an agent that can act. SelfOp builds on these ideas by optimizing the context layer of a frozen agent rather than its weights or harness.

Researchers present commonsense ranked search (CoRS), a path planner that turns abstract instructions such as "move carefully" into routes that respect unstated commonsense considerations. CoRS uses LLMs and VLMs to derive a per-region consideration from visual observations, compare regions pairwise, and sort them into a commonsense ranking whose costs drive a conventional search that always returns a valid route. Experiments show CoRS discovers unstated considerations, detours around those worth avoiding, and crosses the rest, a behavior recent LLM-based planners do not achieve; the work is a preprint and its impact is not yet validated by the community.

## [Benign-Case Cost of Memory-Poisoning Defenses in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22818) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22818) measures the utility and token overhead of memory-poisoning defenses in LLM agents under entirely benign traffic, using a setup that holds the memory backend, retrieval process, and judge constant while varying only the defense. Across three write-time defenses (input sanitization, provenance checking, LLM-based anomaly detection) and one read-time defense (reranking), the write-time defenses show no resolvable utility cost, with 95% confidence intervals of roughly ±4.5 points that include zero, while the reranker lowers core accuracy by 4.4 points and falsely quarantines legitimate memories on 33.6% of adjudicated items. Security evaluations of LLM agent defenses typically focus only on attack prevention, ignoring the cost paid on every benign interaction, so this measurement gives practitioners deploying persistent-memory agents concrete evidence about which defenses are essentially free and which carry real utility and token penalties. It also suggests that where a defense intercepts the pipeline, rather than whether it uses an LLM, determines its benign-case price. The study runs each condition three times across five conversations to separate real effects from pipeline noise, which remains significant even at temperature zero; the reranker's accuracy drop of 4.4 points (95% CI [-9.0, -0.05], bootstrap; McNemar p=0.064) survives replication but sits at the edge of resolution, and its clearer cost is mechanical, reaching as many as 106 false quarantines in a single conversation at 2.7% token overhead. Stacking all four defenses does not compound the cost, as the combined condition's accuracy loss is smaller and its confidence interval includes zero, suggesting write-time defenses may partly offset what the reranker discards.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents increasingly use persistent memory to store facts and preferences across sessions, which creates a memory-poisoning risk: a single adversarial memory write can durably influence agent behavior long after the original conversation ends. Defenses against this are usually split into write-time defenses, which screen incoming memory records before storage, and read-time defenses such as reranking, which reorder or filter retrieved memories based on relevance. Because most real traffic is benign, the cost of these defenses is paid on every interaction while their benefit appears only in rare attacks, making benign-case measurement important.

## [Study Tests Construct Validity of Valence Directions in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22850) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22850) tests whether contrastive activation directions in LLM agents represent intended constructs or merely correlated features, using a maze task with controlled interventions that separate realized outcomes from the informational history through which they became known. Across multiple LLM checkpoints, directions fitted on one explicit outcome encoding transfer well to another, but transfer degrades substantially when the same outcome is reached through announced versus unannounced histories, showing the post-event readout remains conditioned on earlier announcements. ## [Threat Model and Defense Architecture for Prompt Injection in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22949) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.22949) constructs a threat model for prompt injection in multi-agent LLM systems, enumerating 14 attack vectors across four categories: direct user input (3), indirect tool outputs (4), inter-agent message passing (4), and cascading orchestrator manipulation (3). Testing against a 6-agent production-representative system, the authors find 67% of agents vulnerable to at least one scope violation even with system-prompt-level guardrails, and indirect injection via tool outputs succeeds in 43% of attempts. As multi-agent LLM architectures move from research prototypes to production deployments, this work shows that perimeter-style prompt injection defenses designed for single-model chatbots are insufficient because inter-agent message passing, shared tool access, and trust propagation create internal attack surfaces. The proposed four-layer defense architecture reduces overall injection success from 31.2% to 4.2%, offering a concrete blueprint for teams building agentic systems. The four architectural defenses are message signing with provenance tracking (inter-agent injection down 91%), input/output sanitization at agent boundaries (indirect injection down 78%), privilege-scoped tool access per agent role (privilege escalation eliminated entirely), and anomaly detection on inter-agent communication patterns (84% of cascading attempts caught). The paper is an arXiv preprint and has not yet undergone peer review.

**Background**: Prompt injection is an attack where malicious instructions hidden in input or tool output cause an LLM to deviate from its intended behavior. In single-model chatbot settings, defenses typically inspect the user input at one boundary before it reaches the model. Multi-agent systems, where multiple LLM agents collaborate via message passing and shared tools, have many such boundaries, and most are not near the user, making injection harder to detect and contain.

## [Quantum Transformer Blocks Made Interpretable via Hilbert-Space Metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23016) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.23016) shows that Quantum Transformer Blocks (QTB) — fully-coherent variational circuits with quantum analogues of attention and feedforward — can be made interpretable by tracking quantum mutual information (MI), entanglement entropy, and state fidelity through their layers. On four synthetic tasks with known dependency structure, learned MI matrices aligned with ground-truth task structure (AUC = 0.69 on lookup), disabling entangling gates collapsed accuracy from 100% to 15% while MI dropped to zero, and per-sample MI predicted prediction correctness with ROC AUC = 0.84 on a conditional task. This work suggests that quantum machine learning can avoid the opacity of classical deep learning by exploiting quantum mechanics itself as an intrinsic interpretability signal, with no direct classical counterpart. If the advantage persists at scale, it could shape how quantum models are designed, audited, and trusted in domains where explainability is required. All results were validated on IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_kingston, Heron r2), where the circuit's reasoning process — from product state through structured entanglement — was directly observable on a superconducting processor. The authors caution that these are proof-of-concept results on small synthetic tasks, leaving open whether the interpretability advantage persists at scale.

**Background**: Quantum mutual information is the quantum analogue of Shannon mutual information, measuring total correlations (classical and quantum) between subsystems of a quantum state, while entanglement entropy quantifies the degree of entanglement between subsystems via the von Neumann entropy of a reduced density matrix. A Quantum Transformer Block is a variational quantum circuit that mirrors the attention and feedforward structure of classical transformers, and interpretability research seeks to explain how such models process information and why they fail.

## [Testing Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness via Shared Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23065) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.23065) proposes casting chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness as internal concept grounding, encoding both a direct prediction pass and a CoT pass with a single shared sparse autoencoder (SAE) so their latent concepts become directly comparable. It introduces three correlational alignment metrics plus a causal metric, Δp, which ablates shared concepts and measures the resulting drop in answer probability across five LLMs and four datasets. Prior faithfulness work mostly relied on input-output behavior or input attributions, leaving the model's internal computation largely unexplored; this method offers a causal test of whether the concepts underlying a CoT actually drive the prediction. The finding that causal faithfulness peaks at mid-to-late layers rather than final layers, and that causally important concepts are not always verbalized, suggests surface-level or representational correspondence alone cannot reliably assess faithfulness. The correlational metrics show concept alignment is generally high across models and datasets, but they only identify which concepts are shared, not how much they causally contribute; Δp fills that gap. Causal faithfulness varies substantially with model depth, peaking at mid-to-late layers, and model scale reshapes the layer-wise profile, while causally important shared concepts are not always verbalized in the CoT.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Chain-of-thought prompting asks a large language model to produce step-by-step reasoning before answering, which often improves accuracy, but the stated reasoning may not reflect the model's actual internal process — a problem known as CoT unfaithfulness. Sparse autoencoders are interpretability tools that decompose a model's internal activations into sparse, more human-interpretable latent features, approximating the concepts the model uses. This paper combines the two ideas: it uses one shared SAE to compare the concepts active during direct answering versus CoT reasoning, then ablates shared concepts to test whether they causally affect the answer.

## [Neural Spectral Capacity Scores Architectures Without Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23087) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.23087) proposes Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC), a closed-form scalar derived from the singular-value spectrum of each weight matrix that can be computed from an architecture's specification alone, with no model instantiation, data, or gradients. The authors also introduce NSC-DP, an exact dynamic-programming solver that finds the architecture globally maximizing NSC under resource constraints in seconds on a CPU. Standard scalars like #Params and #FLOPs cannot distinguish architectures with identical budgets but different depth-width, head, or FFN allocations, so NSC offers a training-free way to rank and design models. If it holds up, it could speed up neural architecture search and model compression, letting practitioners pick efficient Transformer or CNN designs without expensive training runs. Under standard random initialization, the Marchenko-Pastur law makes NSC computable from architectural specification alone, and its layer-wise additive structure enables the exact NSC-DP solver. Empirically NSC outperforms #Params, #FLOPs, and representative training-free proxies across seven Transformer and CNN families, discovers a Transformer-XL architecture on WikiText-103 that beats the human-designed baseline in 2 seconds, and prunes LLaMA-7B to a 5.7B model without calibration data about 5900x faster than the strongest training-free proxy baseline.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Neural architecture search (NAS) automates the design of neural networks, but most methods require training candidate models or rely on proxy metrics that only capture size and compute. Random matrix theory, specifically the Marchenko-Pastur law, describes the asymptotic distribution of singular values of large random matrices, and prior work has observed that trained Transformer weight matrices deviate from this law at both the largest and smallest singular values. NSC builds on this by using the singular-value spectrum of weight matrices as a structural capacity measure that can be evaluated before any training.

## [DiagGen Turns a Single Image into Simulation-Ready Deformable Assets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23103) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DiagGen is an agentic framework that converts a single in-the-wild image into a simulation-ready deformable asset through a generate-simulate-diagnose-refine loop. It builds part-aware geometry and material parameters, then uses a vision-language model (VLM) agent to select semantically informative regions, probe them in a physics simulator, observe material responses, and route evidence-backed repair cues back to the responsible generation stage. Most existing asset generation pipelines only check physical plausibility after the fact, so an object's simulated response is never used to fix upstream errors; DiagGen closes that loop and shows its deformables can be dropped directly into a high-fidelity simulator for contact-rich pick-and-place planning. Experiments on 40 assets show the diagnostics provide useful repair cues and can moderately improve the quality of generated deformable assets, though the improvement is described as only moderate. The authors contrast DiagGen with assets from visual foundation models, which may not be simulatable at all, and provide a project website at https://diaggen.github.io/.

## [Whitening Inverts Spectral Hierarchy, Breaking Norm-Based Likelihood](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23117) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.23117) shows that whitening foundation-model embeddings systematically over-disperses the squared norm relative to a Gaussian reference, across multiple encoders and three training objectives. The authors trace this to whitening reversing the encoder's spectral hierarchy, shifting norm contributions toward near-degenerate noise directions, and demonstrate that the commonly reported agreement between empirical and theoretical norm statistics is merely an algebraic artifact of in-sample whitening. This challenges a widespread practice in representation learning and generative modeling where the squared norm of whitened embeddings is used as a training-free likelihood surrogate. The findings suggest that Gaussian tail thresholds can be off by orders of magnitude, which could lead to miscalibrated anomaly detection, density estimation, and sample ranking in downstream applications. The paper estimates the dominant input-dependent scale from two moments and uses it to predict cross-dependence between disjoint spectral halves without additional free parameters. It concludes that the squared whitened norm is better interpreted as a Mahalanobis measure of semantic atypicality than as a log-likelihood, explaining both its practical effectiveness in ranking atypical samples and its calibration failures.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Whitening is a linear transform that decorrelates and normalizes embedding coordinates so their covariance becomes the identity, and it is widely used in self-supervised representation learning and contrastive sentence embedding. Practitioners observed that whitened coordinates often look approximately standard normal, motivating the use of the squared norm as a Gaussian likelihood surrogate. The projection central limit theorem explains why individual whitened coordinates can appear normal even when the joint distribution is not Gaussian, which is the key gap this paper addresses.

GrapeSplat introduces a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting method that reconstructs renderable scenes from unposed, uncalibrated images in a single forward pass without per-scene optimization. It combines an Atlas Encoder that lifts views into pixel-wise geometry-and-appearance features, a PEACH-Vox module that compands the unbounded scene into a bounded sparse grid with an exact closed-form inverse, and a Sparse Decoder that decodes multiple Gaussians per occupied voxel cell. This work addresses two key limitations of existing feed-forward Gaussian Splatting methods: fragile global structure caused by purely photometric supervision and pixel-by-pixel prediction, and primitive counts tied to image resolution and view count. By grounding Gaussians in a sparse voxel grid, GrapeSplat could influence future 3D reconstruction research toward more scalable, resolution-independent scene representations. GrapeSplat is trained with both 2D and 3D supervision on 8-view sequences and generalizes zero-shot from 4 to 64 views across indoor and unbounded scenes. In its amalgamated representation, the Gaussian count follows occupied cells and saturates as views cover the scene, while grid resolution sets the ceiling; code and trained weights are available at https://github.com/VAISR/GrapeSplat.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: 3D Gaussian Splatting is a volume rendering technique, revitalized in 2023 by a research group from Inria, that represents scenes as collections of 3D Gaussians and enables real-time radiance field rendering from multiple images. Feed-forward variants aim to predict such Gaussian scenes directly from input images without the slow per-scene optimization that original methods require. Sparse voxel convolution is a technique that applies convolutions only to occupied voxels in a grid, making 3D deep learning more memory- and compute-efficient.

## [CROSS-MAP Decouples Semantics from Structure for Private LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23193) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.23193) proposes CROSS-MAP, a bidirectional framework that replaces the semantics of private inputs with alternative content while preserving the structural information LLMs need for reasoning, then recovers the corresponding outputs afterward. Local models are trained with multi-objective optimization to maximize semantic divergence during mapping and minimize semantic inconsistency during recovery, and experiments show it reduces reconstruction success across multiple attack settings while outperforming existing baselines in utility. As LLM APIs become embedded in privacy-sensitive workflows such as healthcare, legal, and enterprise data processing, users currently must choose between task utility and inference-time privacy. CROSS-MAP's semantic decoupling approach suggests that strong privacy and high downstream performance may not be mutually exclusive, which could influence how future privacy-preserving inference systems are designed. The framework relies on locally trained models rather than modifying the remote LLM API, and it is evaluated against multiple reconstruction attacks while measuring utility against existing baselines. However, the paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review, and the truncated abstract limits assessment of its full experimental scope and real-world deployment constraints.

**Background**: LLM APIs typically require sending raw user prompts to a remote server, which creates a risk that the provider or an attacker could reconstruct sensitive input text. Existing privacy approaches usually keep most of the original semantic content to preserve task performance, but that same content provides cues for reconstruction attacks. Semantic decoupling is an alternative idea: replace the meaning of the input with unrelated content while keeping the structural patterns the model needs to reason correctly, then map the output back to the original domain.

## [LLM Explainers Fail to Flag Corrupted Beliefs in Active Inference Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23215) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper audits LLM explainers attached to an Active Inference (AIF) agent that tracks German grid demand, testing three backends (GPT-4o, Claude-3-Opus, Gemini) with three black-box triggers. Corrupting the observation stream by 600 MW per step shifted the agent's posterior by 490 MW, yet none of the 30 explanations flagged the corruption, and all three explainers produced sycophantic rationalizations for wrong actions 80-95% of the time. This work exposes a critical gap in AI oversight: operators relying on LLM-generated explanations as runtime oversight may be misled by fluent but false accounts of an agent's beliefs and actions. The findings suggest that testing the explainer itself must be part of any audit of an agentic deployment, with direct implications for AI safety in high-stakes domains like power grids. Attacker-controlled text in the observation metadata field was able to steer the explainer, with susceptibility varying by provider and data exfiltration succeeding on all three backends. The paper proposes mitigations for each failure mode but does not evaluate them, and notes that nothing in the explainer architecture checks whether an explanation is true before an operator acts on it.

## [Kernel Theory Explains How Ghost Outputs Teach Subliminal Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23260) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.23260) derives a chained cross-task kernel that mathematically links ghost-output supervision to changes in a student model's task predictions through shared backbone representations. The framework explains three empirical puzzles of Subliminal Learning: the strictly positive semi-definite transfer operator under shared initialization, the rank bottleneck imposed by ghost-output dimensionality, and why high-entropy random noise outperforms structured data as a subliminal transfer probe. This is the first learning-dynamics-based theoretical explanation of subliminal learning, a phenomenon where models acquire downstream capabilities from seemingly unrelated teacher outputs without ever seeing task labels or original data. It matters for AI safety and distillation pipelines, since unintended traits or hidden knowledge could propagate through model training even when developers filter explicit task data. The analysis shows that under shared initialization the transfer operator forms a strictly Positive Semi-Definite (PSD) structure, guaranteeing ghost-output optimization aligns the student with the teacher's true task objective without explicit label exposure. Ghost-output dimensionality acts as an explicit rank bottleneck governing which task-relevant features transfer, and synthetic high-entropy inputs act as broadband probes that maximize cross-task kernel overlap; experiments on the canonical ghost-output setting validate all three predictions.

**Background**: Subliminal Learning (SL) is a recently identified phenomenon in which a student model acquires downstream task capabilities by matching seemingly unrelated auxiliary outputs, called ghost outputs, from a teacher model, despite never observing task labels, task-specific outputs, or the original training data. Prior work identified where subliminal signals may reside, but the optimization mechanism behind the effect remained poorly understood. Kernel methods are a classical tool in machine learning theory that describe how learning dynamics depend on similarities between data points, and this paper extends that lens to cross-task transfer.

## [ValueDiff: Value-Geometric KV Cache Eviction for Sink-Suppressed LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23314) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ValueDiff, a KV cache eviction method that ranks tokens by the L2 deviation of their value vectors from the cache mean, rather than relying on attention scores. On RULER with a tight 2k token budget it retains 88–99% of dense performance across seven sink-suppressed models, and on LongBench at a 4k budget it averages 92% retention versus 83% for the strongest prior baseline. Modern LLMs using QK-normalization, gated attention, learned attention sinks, or logit softcapping exhibit weaker persistent attention sinks, which undermines existing eviction methods that depend on sink tokens. ValueDiff offers a query-invariant, value-side signal that could improve memory-efficient long-context inference for these increasingly common architectures. The same score emerges as the minimal-disturbance eviction under a max-entropy assumption about future attention, and evaluation uses fixed cache budgets with eviction at every block boundary during prefill and every decoding step during generation. On MATH-500 at a 25% cache budget, ValueDiff is the strongest non-dense method on every sink-suppressed model tested, beating prior methods by up to about 20 points on gated-attention models.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: KV cache stores previously computed key-value pairs so an LLM does not reprocess the same context, but it grows with sequence length and becomes a memory bottleneck. Eviction methods keep only a fixed-size subset of tokens, and most prior approaches rely on attention sinks—initial tokens that absorb disproportionate attention regardless of semantics. ValueDiff instead exploits the observation that in sink-suppressed models, value vectors are more dispersed than key vectors, making value geometry a more reliable eviction signal.

## [Patient World Model Forecasts Digital Health Campaign Outcomes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23333) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.23333) introduces a compact patient world model that maintains a per-patient latent state and learns exposure-conditioned dynamics jointly with a weekly conversion hazard, rolling forward into future conversion curves. Evaluated on a US campaign dataset of 147,173 patients and 5.2 million at-risk person-weeks, it forecasts remaining new-to-brand prescription volume through week 52 with relative errors of 2.9% from a week-4 cutoff and 0.8–2.6% from cutoffs at weeks 8–26, far outperforming the strongest non-recurrent baseline (13.6–33.1%). This work reframes in-flight campaign forecasting from a collection of per-cutoff classifiers into a single dynamic-system rollout, which could make real-time measurement of digital health campaigns far more accurate and efficient. A Fisher-information analysis motivates dense next-exposure supervision when conversions are rare; removing this auxiliary objective increases prescription-volume error by roughly 2–14×, with no consistent disadvantage on the more common specialist-visit outcome. The authors also show that switching all future exposure off raises predicted conversion from 0.31 to 0.89, a pattern consistent with selection effects in observational exposure data, highlighting the limits of interpreting exposure-conditioned rollouts causally.

A new arXiv paper proposes the Belief Flow Filter (BFF), a generative filtering framework that updates flow matching model weights via gradient descent at test time to track the evolution of the posterior distribution in Bayesian filtering. Unlike prior generative filtering methods, BFF avoids particle-based posterior representations and trajectory-level inverse problems, and it is empirically validated on five physical systems, including chaotic dynamics, sparse nonlinear observations, and a real-world tokamak plasma estimation task. Bayesian filtering is central to online state estimation in robotics, control, and signal processing, but scaling it to high-dimensional states with complex posteriors remains difficult. By encoding the posterior directly into model weights, BFF offers a potentially more scalable and flexible alternative to particle filters and Gaussian approximations, which could benefit researchers in probabilistic machine learning, state estimation, and generative modeling. The paper theoretically justifies that the BFF design is structurally aligned with Bayesian filtering, with a training objective targeting the recursive filtering operator. Empirically, BFF achieves the best score in 8 of 9 metric-benchmark cells across three standard 1D and 2D PDE benchmarks, and also leads on an extreme single-moving-sensor setting and the tokamak plasma estimation task.

**Background**: Bayesian filtering, also known as recursive Bayesian estimation, is a probabilistic approach for estimating an unknown probability density function over time using incoming measurements and a process model. ## [PhysReflect Uses Geometry and Perception Losses to Fix Mirror Reflections in Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23442) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PhysReflect introduces a geometry and perception guided diffusion framework that decodes predicted clean latents into pixel space at each training step and applies two annealed differentiable objectives: a Geometric Loss using sparse epipolar correspondence and dense boundary projection alignment with a SAM2-based TwinTrack mechanism, and a Perceptual Loss combining DINOv2-based Semantic Consistency with depth, surface-normal, and illumination-based Lighting Consistency. By enforcing reflection-specific geometric and perceptual constraints directly in pixel space, PhysReflect offers a more physically grounded approach to image generation that could improve downstream applications requiring physical plausibility. The method differs from prior work that relies on synthetic data scaling or auxiliary depth conditioning, since those approaches use latent-space noise reconstruction losses as only implicit supervision and cannot directly enforce reflection-specific constraints. PhysReflect instead decodes latents to pixel space and applies annealed supervision through complementary differentiable geometric and perceptual objectives.

## [RLVR²: Verifiable Rubric-Based Ranking for Multi-Dimensional RL Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23457) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper proposes RLVR² (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking), which replaces the common practice of normalizing and linearly combining multiple rubric criterion scores into a single scalar reward with a criterion-specific ordinal ranking approach. Instead of using raw score magnitudes, RLVR² converts rubric scores into within-group ordinal outcomes per criterion, recovers a latent utility from the resulting comparison matrix, and merges these utilities into one training signal. This matters because rubric-based RLVR is increasingly used for tasks with multifaceted quality requirements, where naive scalar aggregation can distort how quality dimensions trade off during training. By avoiding unreliable cross-criterion calibration, RLVR² could improve how reinforcement learning is applied to complex, multi-dimensional objectives in AI/ML, particularly for RLHF and reward modeling. RLVR² retains only within-group ordering and discards raw score magnitudes, which avoids calibrating heterogeneous rubric scales; it also supports objective-preserving attribute adjustment, allowing auxiliary attributes correlated with observed rankings but not training objectives to enter the estimation without expanding the rubric or rewarding them directly. Across three model scales and 16 benchmarks, it consistently outperforms representative rubric-based baselines, achieving the best overall performance on most benchmarks at every scale.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is a paradigm that uses objective, programmatically verifiable rewards—such as checking whether a math answer is correct or whether code passes unit tests—to train models, rather than relying solely on human preference. As RLVR expands to tasks with multifaceted quality requirements, rubric-based reinforcement learning replaces traditional scalar rewards with structured, multi-criteria rubrics. However, policy optimization consumes one scalar per rollout, so rubric-based pipelines must map multiple criterion scores into a single scalar reward, and the prevailing normalization-plus-linear-combination approach assumes cardinal score differences are comparable across criteria and that gains on one criterion can compensate for failures on another.

## [RPMem Brings Reusable Cross-Session Parametric Memory to LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23466) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.23466v2) introduces RPMem, a two-stage architecture that compiles each agent session into a model-independent latent memory via forward computation and selectively merges it with retained memory through a task-trained recurrent gate. The consolidated memory is then mapped to backbone-specific LoRA parameters, and on the PERMA benchmark with Qwen3-8B, RPMem reaches 85.52%, beating the strongest parametric and text-based baselines by 5.32 and 12.98 percentage points respectively. Long-running LLM agents currently rely on text-based memory that re-retrieves and re-reasons over growing histories, so performance degrades as retrieval quality becomes the bottleneck; RPMem instead encodes experience directly into model computation with near-constant update cost and memory footprint. Because the latent memory is model-independent and only the final LoRA mapping is backbone-specific, memory can be reused after the underlying model is replaced, which matters for anyone building agents that must run across many sessions and survive model upgrades. Evaluation spans three long-term memory benchmarks and five diverse backbones, and ablations confirm that session compilation and cross-session consolidation play complementary roles, while dynamics analyses show the recurrent gate learns task-specific memory integration strategies. The abstract is truncated and no community discussion is available, so the full limitations and reproducibility of the reported gains have not yet been independently validated.

**Background**: LLM agents that operate over long horizons need memory that persists and evolves across sessions. Text-based memory stores past interactions as text and retrieves them at query time, which makes long-horizon performance increasingly dependent on retrieval quality and contextual reasoning as histories grow, while parametric memory encodes experience directly into model weights but existing methods offer limited cross-session evolution and are tightly coupled to one backbone. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes pre-trained weights and injects trainable low-rank matrices into Transformer layers, and gated recurrent mechanisms such as the GRU use gates to control information flow and model long-term dependencies in sequential data — RPMem combines both ideas to consolidate and transfer memory.

Building on it, the authors propose StyleAT, an adversarial training scheme that uses low-budget attack variants yet defends against stronger and unseen semantic attacks, evaluated on two unseen datasets and seven models. Face recognition is widely deployed in authentication and surveillance, so vulnerabilities to semantic edits such as aging or pose changes pose real security risks. By making attack generation fast enough for adversarial training, this work could enable more practical defenses for biometric systems. BoundStyle maximizes misclassification by searching StyleGAN's rich latent space, and StyleAT trains on low-budget attack variants while still defending against stronger, unseen semantic attacks. The evaluation covers two datasets unseen during training and seven models, with StyleAT improving robust accuracy over common defenses.

## [PREM: Prefix-Steered Recurrent Memory for Long-Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23601) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PREM introduces a memory-token-free framework for frozen vision-language models that uses a recurrent writer to distill video streams into a compact 256 KiB multi-slot associative state, paired with a question-conditioned readout that adds memory-derived K/V steering modulations to existing non-visual prompt prefixes during prefill. Under a 16-frame budget, it improves macro-average accuracy by 3.06% on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with gains of 11.0% on action antonym identification and 9.9% on localized needle retrieval, while tuning only 0.24% of backbone parameters at 0.03 GiB peak GPU memory overhead. Long-video understanding is bottlenecked by strict token budgets, and PREM shows that a frozen VLM can be substantially improved without appending memory tokens or modifying internal KV caches, enabling write-once, query-many inference. This matters for efficient multimodal systems where the same video must answer many questions cheaply, and it offers a lightweight alternative to full fine-tuning or cache-editing approaches. PREM separates video ingestion from query answering: the recurrent writer compresses visual streams into a 256 KiB associative state, and the readout steers existing non-visual prompt prefixes during prefill, so no extra prompt tokens or decoding recurrence are needed. It was evaluated across six long-video benchmarks in both offline and streaming end-of-stream settings, consistently outperforming frozen baselines at every evaluated visual budget.

## [First Smoothed Analysis of A* with Inconsistent Heuristics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23680) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper presents the first smoothed analysis of the A* search algorithm when using inconsistent heuristics, proving that the expected total number of iterations is bounded by a polynomial O(n²mκ) under slight random perturbations to edge weights. It also shows the result extends to Dijkstra's algorithm on negative-weight graphs. This bridges a long-standing gap between the worst-case exponential bound of inconsistent A* and its efficient practical performance, giving theoretical justification for using powerful machine-learning-derived heuristics that are often inconsistent. It could encourage broader adoption of such heuristics in AI search applications and guide future algorithm design. The bound O(n²mκ) depends on n (nodes), m (edges), and κ, which controls the scale of random perturbations; the analysis models real-world noise by perturbing edge weights of worst-case graphs. The result also applies to Dijkstra's algorithm on negative-weight graphs, which is functionally equivalent to inconsistent A*.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: A* is a fundamental path-finding algorithm that uses a heuristic to estimate the cost to the goal; when the heuristic is admissible and consistent, each state is expanded at most once, guaranteeing efficiency. However, modern applications often use inconsistent heuristics from machine learning or randomized evaluations, which can cause catastrophic node re-expansions and a worst-case exponential time complexity of Ω(2ⁿ). Smoothed analysis is a hybrid of worst-case and average-case analysis that measures expected performance under slight random perturbations of worst-case inputs, explaining why algorithms like the simplex method perform well in practice despite poor worst-case bounds.

## [STEVE Stabilizes Textual-Gradient Prompt Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23716) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced STEVE, a stabilization framework for textual-gradient prompt optimization that combines Error-Driven Refinement, which generates gradients only from incorrectly handled examples, with Regularized Verification, which accepts an update only if hard-case gains do not cause unacceptable regression on a preservation set. Across ten reasoning benchmarks, three evaluator/optimizer models, and established baselines, STEVE reduced performance degradation and produced more robust prompts, with gains persisting in additional tests using gpt-5.4-mini/gpt-5.4 on symbolic reasoning, GSM8K-Platinum, and DS-1000. Textual-gradient prompt optimization is a leading automated alternative to manual prompt engineering, but its iterative updates are known to be unstable, which limits reliability in production LLM pipelines. By directly targeting two identified instability sources, STEVE offers a practical recipe that could make automated prompt optimization more dependable for researchers and practitioners building reasoning systems. The paper attributes instability to two causes: noisy gradients produced from already-correct examples, and over-specialization to hard cases that degrades performance on simpler inputs. STEVE treats every update as provisional and validates it against a preservation set, and the authors report that benefits hold with newer models and larger test sets.

**Background**: Textual-gradient methods automate prompt optimization by having an LLM critique its own outputs in natural language and iteratively rewrite the prompt, analogous to gradient descent but operating on text rather than numeric parameters. This approach is one of several automatic prompt optimization families, alongside score trajectories, genetic evolution, and meta-prompting.
