## [TriFleetRCA: On-Premise LLM Root Cause Analysis for Kubernetes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23766) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TriFleetRCA is an on-premise LLM pipeline that runs entirely on a single workstation GPU to perform Kubernetes root cause analysis, collecting evidence at pod, namespace, or cluster scope, ranking it via template de-duplication followed by BM25, and filtering runbooks through an ingest guard. Evaluated on a live cluster with four injected faults across 100 analyses using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct at temperature 0, it achieved hit rates of 0.85, 0.90, and 0.95 at pod, namespace, and cluster scope, with a median latency of 1.6 seconds at 2,200 prompt tokens. This work addresses a practical constraint for many operators who cannot send production logs to hosted models, showing that useful root cause analysis is feasible on a single on-premise GPU. It also highlights that separating citation quality from diagnostic accuracy can reveal failure modes that accuracy alone conceals, which is important for building trustworthy AIOps systems. The scope effect was driven entirely by one fault whose cause was a cluster-level object, and cluster scope cost 55% more tokens; de-duplication before ranking raised the hit rate from 0.75 to 0.90 at equal token cost. A poisoned runbook instructing the model to delete the namespace was rejected by the guard every run, but with the guard disabled the model declined to follow it in all 20 analyses, making the guard defence in depth rather than the sole barrier.

## [FLARE: Full-Lifecycle Dense Supervision for Long-Horizon Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23808) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose FLARE (Full-Lifecycle Alignment and Reward Engine), a dense supervision paradigm driven by a lightweight Generative Reward Model (GRM) that provides real-time step-level risk feedback for long-horizon coding agents. Its offline RADAR framework distills the GRM via causal-chain backtracking, and FLARE then uses it during inference as an Active Scaffold and during post-training as process-supervised reranking scores for SFT and step-level dense rewards for RL. Sparse Pass/Fail rewards create a severe credit assignment crisis in long-horizon software engineering agents, wasting failed exploratory trajectories and making training costly. FLARE claims a new Pareto frontier across the agent lifecycle, with FLARE (N=1) outperforming Global Rollout (N=5) at 5x lower token consumption, plus 19.13% relative SFT gains and a consistent 9.19% RL improvement. RADAR performs causal-chain backtracking to extract hindsight-free supervision, and the resulting GRM intercepts high-risk generation steps for localized breakpoint re-execution to cut compute overhead. The work is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.23808v1) without peer review or community discussion, so its reported gains remain to be independently verified.

## [ReVeal: Reconstruction-Aware Real-to-Sim Framework for VLA Policy Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23910) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present ReVeal, a real-to-sim assessment framework that combines workspace reconstruction, reconstruction-level fidelity assessment, and matched closed-loop policy evaluation. It introduces two new metrics, Novel-View Mesh Fidelity (NVMF) and Annotated Planar Geometry Fidelity (APGF), plus a depth-supervised reconstruction pipeline called PGSR-D, validated across 8 assessment scenes and 8 humanoid manipulation tasks with GR00T, SmolVLA, and pi0.5. Simulation-based evaluation is a scalable alternative to costly real-world robot testing, but reconstruction errors can make simulated VLA policy performance diverge from reality. ReVeal provides a way to quantify reconstruction fidelity and shows that higher fidelity correlates with stronger real-sim agreement, helping the robotics and embodied AI community judge when simulated evaluations can be trusted. NVMF measures observation fidelity while APGF measures planar geometric fidelity, and across 8 scenes both metrics consistently distinguish the fidelity of 2DGS, PGSR, and PGSR-D. PGSR-D adds monocular depth supervision to improve geometry where multi-view visual cues are limited, and matched evaluations of GR00T, SmolVLA, and pi0.5 show consistent ordering between reconstruction fidelity and real-sim performance agreement.

## [MCPGen: New Executable Benchmark Tests LLMs on End-to-End MCP Workflow Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23925) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint introduces MCPGen, an executable benchmark containing 100 self-contained MCP projects across 16 application domains, designed to test whether LLMs can produce workflow artifacts that stay consistent across graph structure, tool implementation, schema bindings, and runtime wiring. Evaluating 11 representative LLMs in a single-turn setting, the study finds models reach 88.5% on workflow reconstruction but no model exceeds 57% end-to-end execution success, with project-level integration success capped at 45%. As MCP becomes a de facto standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data, this benchmark exposes a critical gap: models that generate plausible-looking workflows often fail when those artifacts must actually execute end-to-end. The finding that integration, not isolated tool generation, is the main bottleneck gives developers and researchers a concrete target for improving agentic coding systems. MCPGen evaluates three diagnostic tasks — workflow reconstruction, tool creation, and backward-compatible workflow extension — using static analysis, unit and integration tests, and process-isolated end-to-end execution. Per-tool unit-test pass rates reach 63.8%, but project-level integration success does not exceed 45%, showing that passing isolated tool tests does not guarantee a working workflow.

RoboTalk introduces a synthetic data-generation pipeline and a dataset of 7,950 multimodal trajectories covering 53 mobile-manipulation kitchen tasks, designed to train small vision-language models (VLMs) to communicate and coordinate in multi-robot settings. Fine-tuning open-source models on this dataset raises success on novel held-out tasks to 77%, compared with roughly 2% for untuned open-source models. The large jump from ~2% to 77% success suggests synthetic multimodal data could be a practical path toward scalable, decentralized robot teams. The dataset includes a leader-follower planning protocol, tool calls for perception, manipulation, navigation, and communication, rationale traces, and diversified natural-language communication. ## [Open-Weight LLMs Misalign Clinical Risk and Cost Tradeoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23999) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv study tested four open-weight LLMs (Qwen-2.5-7B/32B and Llama-3.1-8B/70B) on a public diabetes dataset, varying 11 false-negative to false-positive cost ratios across three phrasings. It found that patient risk was linearly recoverable (AUC ≈ 0.83) and cost direction was recoverable in every model, but only the two larger models showed representational shifts that tracked output changes, and responses to cost magnitude were mostly direction-agnostic. This matters because clinical decision support systems increasingly rely on LLMs, and the study shows that internal knowledge of risk and cost does not translate into cost-correct decisions, especially in smaller models. It suggests clinical evaluations should include tradeoff tests, phrasing sensitivity, and default operating points alongside predictive performance. Only 2 of 12 model-phrasings showed both opposing responses to increasing FN versus FP costs and cost-correct ordering, and a direction fitted on one cost side did not invert when transferred to the other as expected under mirror-symmetric encoding. The study used linear probing to examine internal representations, revealing a gap between what models encode and how they behave.

**Background**: Open-weight LLMs are models whose parameters are publicly available, allowing researchers to inspect their internal representations. ## [SimPrint: Recoverable Semantic Fingerprints for Black-Box LLM Ownership Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24084) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose SimPrint, a recoverable semantic fingerprinting framework that embeds a private owner signature into open-weight LLMs through natural binary question-answering probes rather than isolated secret query-key pairs. Experiments on three open-weight LLMs show the signature can be reliably recovered in both clean and modified settings, remaining robust under fine-tuning, pruning, quantization, model merging, and serving-time perturbations while preserving downstream utility. Open-weight LLMs can be copied, modified, and redeployed behind black-box APIs, making post-release ownership verification a growing problem for model IP protection and AI governance. SimPrint offers a verification method that works purely through input-output queries, so it remains applicable even when model weights or activations are inaccessible. SimPrint encodes the owner signature into a coded semantic fingerprint domain and implants only base-deviating probes via a low-interference batch update that preserves original model behavior. During verification, suspect-model responses are parsed into reliable bits or erasures and decoded with an error-correcting recovery mechanism, which is what allows the signature to survive aggressive model modifications.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Model watermarking and fingerprinting aim to embed hidden ownership information into AI models so that a stolen or copied model can be traced back to its owner. Traditional backdoor-based watermarking embeds behavioral anomalies that can be removed by fine-tuning or pruning, while earlier black-box fingerprints rely on secret query-key pairs that reproduce predefined responses and are easily disrupted by quantization, model merging, or serving-time prompt changes. SimPrint instead distributes ownership evidence across many natural binary question-answering probes, making the fingerprint semantic rather than an isolated exact match.

Benchmark results reveal a substantial ID-OOD gap: uniform memory sampling, increased memory capacity under reliable write policies, proprioceptive inputs, and subtask supervision improve OOD generalization, while planner-guided memory management and decision-making achieve performance close to the best-performing configuration using only sparse memory. A new paper introduces GradCIR, a methodology for training composed image retrieval (CIR) models on graded relevance labels instead of binary relevance. ## [Opinion Leader Dynamics Explains Sparse Attention Token Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24202) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces 'opinion leader dynamics,' a theoretical framework modeling tokens as particles on the unit sphere to analyze how sparse attention induces token clustering and convergence. It formulates two models—explicit (fixed representatives) and implicit (disconnected interaction groups)—as reverse Wasserstein gradient flows and proves exponential convergence under suitable conditions. This provides a rigorous dynamical account of why sparse attention, despite restricting token interactions, can preserve strong empirical performance by supporting within-group alignment while maintaining separation between groups. It bridges theory and practice by connecting predictions to frontier sparse-attention LLMs, offering AI/ML researchers a principled lens on attention sparsity. The paper reports that across four benchmarks, Kimi-K3, MiniMax-M3, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash consistently exhibit clearer cluster separation and higher clustering scores than the dense-attention model GLM-4.7-Flash in projected token representations. Finite-particle simulations illustrate the theoretical convergence behavior, though the analysis relies on idealized conditions for exponential convergence.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Sparse attention reduces the quadratic computational cost of global self-attention in large language models by restricting which tokens interact, but how these restricted interactions shape token representations has been theoretically underexplored. Wasserstein gradient flows describe the evolution of probability measures along trajectories that minimize an objective within the Wasserstein geometry, and reverse Wasserstein gradient flows are used here to model the token dynamics. The unit sphere serves as the state space for token particles, and opinion leader dynamics borrows from social science to explain how representative tokens attract others toward consensus directions.

## [Replication Study Tests How Language Models Recall Facts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24238) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A large-scale replication study tested 31 language models from the Pythia, GPT-2, Qwen3, and Ministral families, confirming that larger models and higher-frequency entities favor memorized answers but finding that entity-frequency effects vanish on Qwen3-14B and 32B and that question phrasing alone can shift reliance on memorized knowledge by up to 80 percentage points. The findings show that many prior conclusions about how language models arbitrate between memorized and in-context knowledge do not generalize cleanly across model families and prompts, which matters for researchers and practitioners who rely on such behavioral claims when designing prompts, evaluating factual recall, or building retrieval-augmented systems. The study extended evaluations beyond world capitals to five additional knowledge relation types from the ParaConflict dataset, and it found that semantically unrelated prose can mimic coherent supporting context, while post-training shifts the memory-context trade-off inconsistently across families.

## [Cross-Hessian Rank Constraint Enables Nonlinear Latent Causal Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24241) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.24241) proposes the cross-Hessian Rank Constraint (HRC), a rank-based primitive for nonlinear latent causal discovery. The authors prove that the rank of the cross-Hessian of the observed-data log-density equals the dimension of the latent variables when two groups of observed variables are d-separated by lower-dimensional latents, and that this reduces to Tetrad constraints in the linear Gaussian case. This work relaxes restrictive assumptions such as linear relations or invertible mixing functions that limit existing latent causal discovery methods, potentially broadening the applicability of causal discovery to general nonlinear settings. It offers a theoretically grounded tool that could benefit researchers in causal inference, representation learning, and related fields. The rank property holds under a mild affine derivative assumption on the conditional log-density derivatives, which is naturally satisfied when noise is low or nonlinearity is moderate. The authors instantiate HRC in the pure one-factor measurement setting to locate latent variables and recover their causal structure up to Markov equivalence, with experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets supporting the theory.

**Background**: Latent variable causal discovery aims to uncover hidden variables and their causal relationships from observed data, a fundamental but challenging problem. Traditional methods often assume linear relationships or invertible mixing functions, which are restrictive for real-world nonlinear systems. Tetrad constraints are classical rank-based conditions used in linear Gaussian latent variable models to test whether observed correlations are consistent with a given latent structure. This paper generalizes such rank-based constraints to the nonlinear case via the cross-Hessian of the log-density.

## [MemCalib Benchmark Exposes LLM Agents' Poor Memory Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24259) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced MemCalib, a benchmark built on realistic memory-system scenarios that evaluates whether an LLM gives each in-context memory an appropriate degree of influence over its response. Testing frontier open- and closed-source models showed they frequently over-use or under-use memory, and that common post-training methods such as GRPO and on-policy self-distillation improve one direction while worsening the other, motivating the proposed MemCalib-RL algorithm. Memory is a core module of LLM agents, and this work shows that even frontier models lack a capability that directly determines response quality, making memory calibration a previously overlooked research target. The finding that popular post-training methods cause directional skew, plus a reinforcement-learning fix that generalizes beyond the benchmark, could reshape how agent memory systems are trained and evaluated. MemCalib-RL is an ordered bidirectional counterfactual credit-assignment algorithm that separates over-use and under-use signals and localizes credit to response tokens via exact atom ablation. Experiments across Qwen3-8B, Ministral-3-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B show it achieves the best overall performance with better balance between over- and under-use, and gains generalize to external benchmarks; the paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community validation yet.

## [vla.simd Brings Real-Time CPU Inference to Robot Manipulation Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24274) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released vla.simd, a CPU inference engine that combines shared SIMD micro-kernels, reusable computation, and target-specific optimization to accelerate language-conditioned manipulation policies. It achieves roughly 1.4x median speedup over compiled PyTorch references across six policies and four CPUs while preserving fp32 fidelity, and the accompanying IMPACT policy supplies 33.5 actions/s in fp32 (81.2 in int8) on a Raspberry Pi 5 after a 90-second thermal soak. This work shows that vision-language-action policies can run in real time on cheap, low-power CPUs without a dedicated GPU, which could substantially lower the cost and power barriers for deploying language-conditioned robots at the edge. It also introduces a way to reason about action supply versus feedback frequency, which matters for any system that must cover policy query latency with action chunks. The engine targets linear layers, convolutions, and attention projections with a shared SIMD micro-kernel plus target-specific tiling and quantization, and the paper distinguishes action supply from feedback frequency under lagged and time-aligned execution. IMPACT is an ACT-based policy with cached text representations and language-modulated visual features, and it is the only language-conditioned policy in the evaluated set to supply at least 30 actions/s on the Raspberry Pi 5; separate GPU evaluations report 76.4% mean success across four LIBERO suites without robot pretraining, with trials on an SO-101 arm and SmolVLA on a UR10e with a Robotiq gripper.

**Background**: Language-conditioned manipulation policies are models that take a natural-language instruction plus visual observations and output robot actions, often built on vision-language-action (VLA) architectures. ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers) is a widely used policy that predicts a chunk of future actions at once, which helps smooth execution but requires the policy to run fast enough to keep supplying new chunks. SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) lets a CPU apply one operation to many numbers at once, and micro-kernels are small hand-tuned compute routines that exploit this for operations like matrix multiplication. Deploying such policies on edge devices like the Raspberry Pi 5 usually means giving up GPUs, so inference efficiency becomes the bottleneck.

## [Temporal Generalization of CFG Neural Networks for Malware Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24280) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper evaluates control flow graph neural networks for malware detection using a strict temporal split, training on 459 graphs from 2024-2025 and testing on 223 graphs from 2026. It finds that the choice of message-passing operator significantly changes robustness to temporal distribution shift, and that a flat-feature control model with no topology is best in-distribution but among the worst across the temporal boundary. Most malware detection benchmarks use random splits from a single time period, which hides how models degrade on future samples; this work shows that operator choice, not just recalibration or ensembling, is critical for real-world robustness. It also warns that the most accurate operator on later data is the hardest to explain, which matters for security analysts who need interpretable detections. The study extracted two corpora of control flow graphs, each node carrying 37 features, from 1,989 Windows portable executables, and trained twelve variants plus a flat-feature control. Every pairwise gap that survives correction separates an aggregating architecture from one built around a learned attentional readout, and attributions do not shift even though explanation validity is architecture-specific.

## [TTSE: A Two-Track Online Self-Evolution Framework for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24289) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.24289) proposes TTSE, a dual-track online self-evolution framework that separates evolving agent knowledge into FACT (environmental facts continuously verified through interaction evidence) and TIP (task-conditioned implementation procedures). The paper provides a decision-theoretic decomposition of the agent's excess risk into environment-representation regret and conditional-execution regret, and validates the approach on GDPevo, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, SOPBench, and PinchBench. Most existing reinforcement learning approaches for LLM agents adapt only to fixed task distributions or single environments, limiting long-term autonomy; TTSE's separation of verified environmental facts from task-specific procedures offers a more general mechanism for continual adaptation. If the results hold up, this could influence how future agent frameworks structure memory, skill evolution, and online learning. The theoretical analysis characterizes when environment-conditioned policies strictly outperform condition-agnostic policies and bounds downstream risk in terms of FACT identification error and cross-condition mismatch cost. Empirically, TTSE is broadly compatible with existing skill self-evolution methods, and when combined with the Bayesian-Agent algorithm it substantially improves the aggregate score across five major domains of SOPBench over three independent repetitions.

Reinforcement learning is a common way to train such agents, but it typically optimizes for a fixed task distribution. ## [KV-COBRA Co-Optimizes Rank and Bit-Width Per Attention Head for KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24298) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KV-COBRA introduces a per-head co-optimization of rank truncation and bit-width for KV-cache compression, formalizing it as a resource-allocation problem that balances rank-truncation loss against quantization loss within each head and redistributes budget across heads to minimize total distortion. It uses a fused Hadamard rotation to equalize per-channel variance and reorders the SVD basis by attention-KL importance to make the solver query-aware, extending to joint K+V compression. This matters because KV-cache memory and bandwidth are major bottlenecks for long-context LLM inference, and KV-COBRA shows that how the compression budget is allocated across attention heads matters more than the choice of compression scheme itself. It achieves the smallest accuracy degradation among evaluated methods at low bit-rates (0.5 to 4 bits per dimension) with no per-token overhead, making it practical for efficient inference deployments. The method relies only on standard low-rank projection and scalar quantization, and it outperforms uniform allocation with the largest gains at low bit-rates. Evaluation covers perplexity, zero-shot, and long-context benchmarks from 0.5 to 4 bits per dimension (bpd), with no per-token overhead.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: KV cache stores the key and value tensors generated during autoregressive LLM inference so they don't need to be recomputed, but its memory footprint grows with sequence length and can dominate GPU memory for long contexts. Compression techniques typically combine low-rank approximation (truncating the rank of the KV matrices) and quantization (reducing bit-width), and prior work applied these uniformly across all attention heads. KV-COBRA's insight is that each attention head has a different optimal mix of rank truncation and quantization, so treating budget allocation as a per-head resource-allocation problem yields better accuracy at extreme compression rates.

A new paper introduces InfoPPO, which reparameterizes temporal progression in the reinforcement learning Markov Decision Process using information density rather than raw token count. Credit assignment in long-horizon reasoning is a known weakness of token-by-token RL for LLMs, since information flow along autoregressive trajectories is highly non-uniform. InfoPPO's information-time formulation could improve RLVR training stability and effectiveness for long reasoning chains, which matters to researchers working on reasoning models and policy optimization. InfoPPO restores the effectiveness of non-trivial discounting in long-horizon reasoning by retaining effective-horizon contraction while avoiding excessive attenuation of terminal supervision over long token sequences. The authors extend performance-difference and policy-improvement analyses to the information-time MDP, deriving a policy-improvement lower bound when policy changes are regulated by information density, and show stable accuracy and response length across non-trivial discount settings where token-time PPO deteriorates.

In standard PPO-style training, the trajectory is treated as a sequence of tokens, so each generated token counts as one time step regardless of how much new information it carries. Because some tokens (like a key reasoning step) matter far more than others (like filler words), this token-count time parameterization can distort credit assignment and discounting over long reasoning chains.

A new paper introduces Attention with Routed Memory (ARM), a fully differentiable, fixed-size KV caching structure organized as a hierarchical router that uses Gumbel-Softmax to learn which memory slots to select and sigmoid-gated updates to softly merge new and stored information. ARM also trains a policy to dynamically choose how much memory to access at inference time, and experiments on commonsense and long-context reasoning benchmarks show better performance and efficiency than fixed KV-caching approaches. KV cache growth is one of the main bottlenecks for long-context LLM inference, and existing eviction or pruning methods often discard core information. ARM's learnable, differentiable memory routing could enable more scalable long-context inference with lower memory and latency, which matters for anyone deploying LLMs on long documents, code, or multi-turn dialogue. ARM keeps the memory size fixed and uses Gumbel-Softmax for differentiable slot selection plus sigmoid gates for soft updates, avoiding hard eviction and reducing information loss. A learned policy further varies the amount of memory accessed per input, so simple contexts use less memory while deeper reasoning inputs can draw on more.

**Background**: In transformer-based LLMs, the key-value (KV) cache stores past attention keys and values so the model does not recompute them for every new token, but this cache grows linearly with sequence length and can consume many gigabytes of memory. Prior work tries to control this by evicting or pruning less important tokens, which is efficient but risks losing information that later tokens may need. Gumbel-Softmax is a technique that makes discrete selection differentiable by relaxing categorical sampling into a soft, temperature-controlled distribution, and sigmoid gates are the same kind of gating used in LSTMs to control how much old versus new information is kept.

## [ActGov Enforces LLM Agent Actions via Policy-Constrained Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24446) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ActGov is a runtime enforcement framework that validates each LLM-proposed tool action before it causes external effects, combining an iterative policy-construction component (ActGov-Policy) with SMT-based counterexample checking and a runtime component (ActGov-Runtime) that abstracts tool calls into finite policy records. Evaluated on the AgentDojo and AgentDyn benchmarks across multiple models and attack configurations, it consistently reduces indirect prompt-injection attack success rates while preserving task utility, outperforming existing defenses. LLM agents increasingly execute long-horizon workflows through external tools, where untrusted outputs can influence later actions and exceed user authorization, and existing defenses that isolate injected content or rely on predefined plans and static policies are brittle under dynamic workflows. ActGov offers a per-action enforcement approach that preserves authorization throughout dynamically branching workflows without relying on the underlying LLM to correctly identify malicious instructions, which is directly relevant to AI safety and systems security in agent deployment. The framework is built on a unified semantic model of authorization, actions, runtime context, and security constraints, and each policy update is verified through SMT-based counterexample checking; at runtime a tool call is permitted only if it remains within the task-scoped authorization boundary and satisfies all applicable policies. The approach is evaluated on AgentDojo and AgentDyn across multiple models and attack configurations, though the abstract does not report specific quantitative numbers or discuss performance overhead.

## [Lifted Bellman Linear Programming Offers New Offline RL Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24489) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP), a novel offline reinforcement learning method that enforces in-sample Bellman optimality via inequality constraints in joint (Q,V) space, yielding a unique minimizer that is invariant to rollout policy and horizon. An approximate neural implementation, ALBUM, matches FQL performance on OGBench with a single critic and Gaussian policy, using the fewest parameters and least peak GPU memory among compared methods. This work could simplify offline RL training by eliminating the need for target networks, EMA updates, and off-policy correction, which are common sources of instability. It provides rigorous theoretical guarantees on the in-sample optimal solution, making it valuable for researchers seeking more stable and efficient offline RL algorithms. Under deterministic dynamics, the LBLP minimizer lies between the best dataset return and the optimal value, and relaxing constraints into hinge penalties recovers the same solution above a finite penalty coefficient in the tabular case. ALBUM detaches K-step rollout targets by stop gradient and can be trained without target networks or EMA updates, with a stationary point condition independent of discount factor and horizon.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn policies from a fixed dataset without environment interaction, which is important in high-stakes applications where exploration is costly or dangerous. Traditional methods train a critic by minimizing regression loss against bootstrapped value targets stabilized by target networks with exponential moving average (EMA) updates, and multi-step targets require off-policy correction. Bellman optimality is a necessary condition for optimality in dynamic programming, and linear programming provides a characterization of it. LBLP lifts this characterization to joint (Q,V) space so that constraints only involve dataset state-action pairs.

A new arXiv paper (2609.24504) systematically studies how model merging affects emergent capabilities across two testbeds — activation oracles and emergent-misaligned models — spanning three model families. ## [iSDFT: Budgeted Self-Distillation Cuts LLM Forgetting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24646) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Information-Proximal Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (iSDFT), which reframes the teacher in on-policy self-distillation as a budgeted information source rather than always distilling toward the full demonstration-conditioned teacher. At each token it selects the distribution closest to the current student that satisfies a prescribed teacher-information constraint, yielding a closed-form exponential target with a locally determined tilt, plus an anchor to the frozen base policy to control cumulative drift. This matters because it addresses a known limitation of SDFT—fixed teacher influence—and shows that controlling how much and when teacher information is introduced improves specialization while preserving broader capability. Across four heterogeneous LLM backbones and two specialization tasks, iSDFT improved vanilla SDFT in 7 of 8 model-task settings and matched it in the remaining one, making it a valuable technical contribution for continual learning and LLM fine-tuning researchers. iSDFT provides tighter retention on the original SDFT benchmark suite, with 73% of evaluations remaining within 0.5 points of the base model versus 52% for the strongest baseline, and it achieves the largest mean improvement on all ten additional mathematics, coding, and competition-mathematics benchmarks. The method's closed-form target and locally determined tilt are notable technical specifics, though the abstract does not detail computational overhead or hyperparameter sensitivity.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy self-distillation fine-tuning (SDFT) is a method that lets models learn new skills from demonstrations while reducing catastrophic forgetting—the tendency of LLMs to lose previously learned abilities when fine-tuned on new data. SDFT always distills toward the full demonstration-conditioned teacher, fixing teacher influence at the full-teacher endpoint and providing no control over how much demonstration information should be transferred at each prediction state. iSDFT builds on this by treating the teacher as a budgeted information source, an information-theoretic approach to continual learning.

## [Corrective Forcing Unifies Post-Training for Diffusion and Flow Speech Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24651) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Corrective Forcing (CoF), a unified post-training paradigm that trains diffusion and flow models for speech enhancement on their own self-generated rollout states rather than only analytical training path states. CoF corrects clean-speech predictions on rollout states toward ground truth under dynamic sampling schedules, and regularizes local evolution using locally corrected counterfactual transitions; experiments with SB-VE and OT-CFM show improved perceptual quality, reconstruction fidelity, and robustness across different sampling step counts. Training-inference mismatch is a known but underexplored problem in diffusion and flow generative models, where errors accumulate during recursive sampling and degrade output quality. A post-training method that works across both diffusion and flow formulations could make generative speech enhancement more reliable and less sensitive to the number of sampling steps, benefiting audio generation research and practical deployment. CoF expresses model outputs through a shared clean-speech prediction parameterization, allowing the same post-training objective to be applied to both diffusion and flow formulations. The method is evaluated with SB-VE (a variance-exploding diffusion variant) and OT-CFM (optimal-transport conditional flow matching), and it maintains robust performance across varying numbers of sampling steps.

## [Tree-Structured Speculative Decoding Adapted to DeepSeek-V4-Flash](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24698) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper integrates tree-structured speculative decoding into the DeepSeek-V4-Flash pipeline using branch-aware causal verification, temporary state isolation, and accepted-path state refresh to keep verification and compressed-state updates consistent across branches. Across budgets D=5 to D=8, batch sizes 1 to 64, and three datasets (GSM8K, MBPP, ShareGPT), tree speculation achieves a higher accepted length than matched linear configurations in all settings (e.g., at D=8 about 2.83–3.41 versus 2.39–2.84) and improves throughput by up to about 18.5%. This work shows that retaining multiple candidate paths under the same budget can effectively improve DeepSeek-V4 decoding efficiency, offering a practical recipe for adapting speculative decoding to models with compressed, sparse, or structured context representations. The reported gains follow stable, transferable regularities, making the approach relevant to researchers and engineers working on efficient LLM inference. The main difficulty lies on the target-verify side: because DeepSeek-V4's CSA/HCA online compressed attention compresses branches diverging from a shared prefix into different states, cross-branch state consistency breaks. The relative gain grows with the budget and is most pronounced for less predictable workloads at small-to-medium batch sizes, but beyond a certain budget throughput plateaus and decouples from the still-rising accepted length.

**Background**: Autoregressive decoding repeatedly runs the target model for each token, which is a major source of LLM inference latency. Speculative decoding speeds this up by having a cheaper draft model propose candidate tokens that the target model then verifies in parallel; linear speculation follows a single candidate chain, while tree-structured speculation keeps multiple branches from shared prefixes to broaden coverage under the same budget. DeepSeek-V4 replaces standard full attention with CSA (Compressed Sparse Attention) and HCA (Heavily Compressed Attention), which compress context online and complicate cross-branch state handling during verification.

## [SPECTRA: Reconfigurable Tiled Chip Speeds Up Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24847) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SPECTRA introduces a runtime-reconfigurable tiled architecture that switches each tile's compute engine between systolic execution for GEMMs and vector-lane execution for GEMVs, and dynamically adapts tile count, kernel partitioning, and communication patterns across tiles on a per-kernel basis. Evaluated on a 20-tile FPGA prototype across the Pythia, SmolLM2, and GPT-2 model families, it achieves up to 2.09x speedup from tile-level reconfiguration and a further 1.25x gain from system-level adaptability over fixed designs. Speculative decoding is a key technique for accelerating LLM inference, but its verification step creates a runtime-dependent regime between memory-bound GEMV and compute-bound GEMM that fixed hardware handles inefficiently. By adapting hardware to this varying arithmetic intensity, SPECTRA points toward more efficient LLM inference on resource-constrained edge devices, benefiting researchers and engineers working on efficient inference systems. The reconfiguration operates at two levels: within each tile the compute engine switches between systolic and vector-lane modes, while across tiles the system selects tile count, kernel partitioning, and communication pattern, both on a per-kernel basis. Results are demonstrated on an FPGA prototype rather than a fabricated ASIC, so real-chip area, power, and clock-frequency tradeoffs remain to be validated.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Autoregressive LLM decoding generates one token at a time and is typically memory-bound, while the prefill phase processes many tokens at once and is compute-bound. Speculative decoding speeds up decoding by having a small draft model propose several tokens that a larger target model then verifies in a single batched pass, but this verification step sits between the two regimes, with arithmetic intensity that varies with speculation length and acceptance rate. Systolic arrays are grids of processing elements well suited to dense matrix multiplication (GEMM), whereas vector-lane designs handle matrix-vector products (GEMV) more efficiently; runtime-reconfigurable tiled architectures divide hardware into small tiles that can be reconfigured on the fly.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.24862) introduces TimEvolve, a frozen-backbone time-series agent that converts each realized forecast outcome into persistent joint updates of expert trust, agent path selection, and intervention strength. Using a temporally ordered predict-reveal-update protocol, it achieves the best average MSE and MAE ranks among fifteen methods across eight Time-MMD domains, with the lowest errors on both metrics in seven domains. This work addresses a real limitation in existing time-series agents, which typically incorporate prior experience only through forecast refinement, reflection, or retrieval rather than systematically updating the orchestration policy itself. By turning deployment outcomes into delayed supervision without extra annotation, it points toward forecasting systems that continuously improve as their underlying mechanisms evolve. The approach commits all numerical expert forecasts and candidate agent paths before target observation, so each realized outcome can evaluate the entire alternative set and provide delayed feedback. The backbone remains frozen, meaning only the joint orchestration policy is updated rather than the underlying forecasting models.

**Background**: Agentic time-series forecasting refers to systems that coordinate multiple numerical models, reasoning strategies, and intervention rules, whose relative effectiveness changes over time as the underlying mechanisms evolve. Traditional forecasting agents adapt mainly by refining forecasts or retrieving past experience, but they do not persistently update the policy that decides which components to trust and how to coordinate them. TimEvolve is positioned against this gap, using the natural delay between making a forecast and observing the realized target as a supervision signal.

## [SE(3) Neural Potential Fields Enable 6-DoF Planning Directly from Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24864) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present an SE(3) neural potential field learned from posed RGB images and supervised with a navigation function—the geodesic distance to the grasp through free space recovered from those same images during training—which removes the classical potential-field failures of grazing and stalling. On two tabletop scenes executed on a UR10, the field converges within 3 cm of the grasp from every start, all executed paths are collision-free against ground-truth geometry, and mean clearance rises from under 1 cm to 8.6–8.8 cm. This work shows that collision-free 6-DoF grasp trajectories can be planned directly from images without an explicit 3D reconstruction, cutting deployed planning time to about 2 s versus 67–133 s for RRT* on a reconstruction of the same images. It matters for robotics practitioners who need fast, reliable motion planning in clutter, and it demonstrates that navigation-function supervision can fix long-standing local-minima and grazing problems of learned potential fields. The method was validated on real UR10 hardware across two tabletop scenes: executed grasp success was 90.0% and 40.0%, with residual failures attributed to refusals of the Cartesian executor rather than the field itself. Under image supervision alone, collision-free rates were only 25% and 0%, and arm-link contacts fell from 20.6–50.4% to 2.7–5.5% of executed configurations; notably, under a common offline harness the learned field and RRT* are comparable, so the deployed margin reflects the cost of collision-checking a dense reconstruction rather than planner complexity.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Artificial potential fields are a classic motion-planning approach that guides a robot toward a goal using attractive and repulsive gradients, but they suffer from local minima where gradients cancel, causing the robot to graze obstacles or stall short of the goal. Neural fields learn continuous representations from data, and SE(3) denotes the special Euclidean group of 3D rotations and translations that describes rigid-body poses. A navigation function is a specially constructed potential function that is bounded, analytic, and guarantees convergence to the goal without spurious local minima, which is why it is used here as a supervisory signal.

## [Iterative Unalignment Estimates Rare Events in AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24969) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces an iterative unalignment method that perturbs a language model's weights to build an importance sampling proposal for estimating rare event probabilities in stochastic AI agents. The approach uses gradient-based search over weight space with a differentiable surrogate for event amplification and adaptive regularization, achieving over 800x compute-weighted efficiency gains over naive Monte Carlo for events rarer than 10^-7. As autonomous agents are deployed more widely, even extremely rare catastrophic events along their stochastic output trajectories can occur, so safe deployment depends on knowing how often they might happen. This work provides a practical tool for AI safety and reliability by making rare-event risk estimation tractable for large language model agents. The method was evaluated on ~120M and ~2.6B parameter models across three event families spanning over 300 rare events as rare as 10^-9, with reference probabilities computed at less than 10% relative standard error. The implementation is available at https://github.com/namkoong-lab/iterative-unalignment.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Rare event estimation is a classic problem in reliability engineering and statistics, where naive Monte Carlo simulation becomes computationally prohibitive because the events of interest are so infrequent. Importance sampling addresses this by sampling from a modified proposal distribution that makes rare events more likely, then reweighting the samples, but constructing an effective proposal is difficult when the event depends on a long chain of conditional distributions. This paper applies that idea to language model agents by treating the model's weights as the parameterization of the proposal and using gradients to search for weights that amplify the rare event while keeping the estimator stable.

The method uses a temporally annealed budget for the proposer, exploration encouragement based on evolution history, and a selector with a critic and pruner, yielding up to 14.1 points on the in-distribution split and up to 4.7 points on five out-of-distribution benchmarks while using 30% fewer policy tokens. Recursive self-improvement of agent harnesses can overfit to training tasks, producing large in-distribution gains that shrink or vanish on out-of-distribution benchmarks. RRSI offers a practical regularization approach that favors reusable agent mechanisms over benchmark-specific ones, which is relevant to researchers and practitioners building generalizable LLM agents. The proposer limits how many edits a candidate can bundle via a temporally annealed budget and encourages unexplored trajectories, while the selector's critic screens benchmark-specific proposals and its pruner removes changes that are too small, too expensive, or no longer useful. This theoretical grounding could guide the design of more efficient and reliable self-improvement pipelines for LLMs, affecting researchers and practitioners working on reasoning, RLHF, and synthetic data generation. The analysis specifies conditions under which a pre-trained model can initiate effective reasoning improvement, shows why policy improvement is iterative, and proves convergence to an optimal reasoning policy. It also demonstrates that STaR remains robust even when incorporating occasional incorrect steps, and the empirical return curves from GPT-2, Qwen2.5-0.5B, and Phi-3-mini align with theoretical predictions.

CARD is a hierarchical framework that clusters users by shared stylistic patterns, learns group-specific LoRA adapters, and captures individual differences via an implicit preference learning mechanism that contrasts user-authored text with cluster-level generations. At inference, it injects personalization only at decoding through lightweight user preference vectors and low-rank logit corrections while keeping the base model frozen, outperforming baselines on the LaMP and LongLaMP benchmarks. This work addresses the tension between fine-grained personalization and scalable deployment, offering a practical path to serve many users efficiently without training a separate model per user. It could benefit applications like personalized email writing, recommendation explanations, and other user-adaptive text generation where low-resource users are common. The framework keeps the base model frozen and only adds lightweight user preference vectors and low-rank logit corrections at decoding time, which significantly improves efficiency and scalability. It also shows strong low-resource performance by leveraging cluster-level generalization, though the approach depends on the quality of user clustering and preference vectors.

## [Survey Maps Agentic Reasoning for LLMs into Three Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12538) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv survey (2601.12538v2) organizes agentic reasoning for large language models into three complementary layers: foundational single-agent reasoning (planning, tool use, search), self-evolving reasoning (feedback, memory, adaptation), and collective multi-agent reasoning (coordination, knowledge sharing, shared goals). It further distinguishes in-context reasoning, which scales test-time interaction through structured orchestration, from post-training reasoning, which optimizes behavior via reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning. Agentic reasoning is one of the most active research areas in LLMs, and this survey provides a unified roadmap that bridges thought and action, helping researchers and practitioners navigate a fragmented landscape. By covering applications in science, robotics, healthcare, autonomous research, and mathematics, it offers a shared vocabulary for building and evaluating autonomous agents. The survey formalizes collective multi-agent reasoning as a decentralized, partially observable multi-agent setting, commonly modeled as a Dec-POMDP, and reviews representative frameworks and benchmarks across real-world domains. It also outlines open challenges including personalization, long-horizon interaction, world modeling, scalable multi-agent training, and governance for real-world deployment.

A new arXiv paper (2602.20628v2) relaxes prior assumptions about how misaligned AIs might collude to subvert untrusted monitoring, introducing a taxonomy of passive self-recognition, causal collusion (hidden pre-shared signals), acausal collusion (Schelling-point signals), and combined strategies. It presents a safety case sketch that states assumptions explicitly and identifies conditions under which passive self-recognition may be more effective than previously studied collusion strategies. The paper builds on existing pre-deployment testing methods for AI control safety cases and explicitly highlights unsolved challenges rather than claiming a complete solution. Its taxonomy distinguishes passive self-recognition, causal collusion, acausal collusion via Schelling points, and combinations, and it argues that passive self-recognition can sometimes outperform the collusion strategies studied in earlier AI control research.

CivBench introduces a new benchmark that evaluates LLM strategists in multiplayer Civilization V by training state-value function estimators to predict the probability of eventual victory from any game state, replacing sparse terminal win/loss signals. The authors cross-evaluated 307 games across 7 LLMs and multiple agent conditions, showing the benchmark is unsaturated and reveals model-specific effects of agentic setup. This work addresses a key gap in LLM evaluation by providing a generative, competitive, and longitudinal environment with dense progress signals, enabling richer assessment of long-horizon strategic decision-making than outcome-only benchmarks. It could influence how researchers design benchmarks for multi-agent, multi-turn tasks and reveal strategic profiles of LLMs that are otherwise invisible. CivBench trains estimators of a state-value function—the probability that a player eventually wins given the game state—to overcome the sparse reward problem in games spanning hundreds of turns. The benchmark is unsaturated, meaning current LLMs do not saturate its performance, and it outlines distinct strategic profiles not visible through outcome-only evaluation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Evaluating strategic decision-making in LLMs requires environments that are generative, competitive, and longitudinal, but few benchmarks offer all three. In reinforcement learning, a state-value function estimates the expected return from a given state, and sparse rewards—where success signals are rare—make learning difficult. Civilization V is a complex turn-based strategy game with multiple opponents and hundreds of turns, making terminal win/loss signals too sparse for effective evaluation.

## [Model-Native Skills: Recovering Interpretable Bases from LLM Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17614) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2604.17614v2) proposes a "model-native" skill characterization method that recovers a compact orthogonal basis directly from sequence-level activations, rather than relying on human-written taxonomies. Validated on reasoning post-training across Llama3-8B and Qwen2.5-3B, the recovered directions improved Pass@1 by up to 20% on MATH and 41% on AMC when used for SFT data selection, and boosted Pass@8 by up to 4.8% on MATH when used as inference-time steering vectors. This work challenges the dominant paradigm of using human-defined skill taxonomies for data curation and model intervention, showing that grounding skills in the model's own representations yields measurably better results. If validated, it could reshape how practitioners approach SFT data selection, inference-time steering, and safety alignment, offering a unified activation-space framework that human-characterized skills cannot support. The method recovers an orthogonal basis from sequence-level activations that is semantically interpretable but need not map onto any predefined human ontology, and lightweight proxy interventions are used to identify which directions are most useful for a given model. The same basis serves dual purposes—SFT data selection and inference-time steering vectors—and was further validated on safety alignment, where selecting adversarial training data for model-native skill coverage proved more sample-efficient than selecting for textual diversity; code is open-sourced.

Using LAPITHS, the authors argue that major claims by models such as CENTAUR, proposed as an artificial Unified Model of Cognition, are not theoretically or empirically justified. LAPITHS integrates two quantitative assessments: the Minimal Cognitive Grid, a theoretically motivated method for estimating the cognitive plausibility of artificial systems, and a behavioural comparison showing that results similar to those reported for CENTAUR-like models can be reproduced by other systems that do not satisfy the structural constraints typically associated with cognitive plausibility.

## [RankQ Uses Self-Supervised Action Ranking for Offline-to-Online RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11151) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RankQ introduces a self-supervised multi-term ranking loss that augments temporal-difference learning in offline-to-online Q-learning, enforcing structured action ordering instead of uniformly penalizing out-of-distribution actions. On sparse-reward D4RL benchmarks it matches or beats seven baselines, and in vision-based robot learning it improves VLA fine-tuning by 38.2 percentage points in low-data simulation and raises real-world cube stacking success from 43.1% to 88.9%. This offers a new way to mitigate value overestimation in offline-to-online RL without the behavior-cloning anchor that limits policy improvement when offline data is suboptimal, which could make fine-tuning of large pretrained policies like VLAs more sample-efficient. The strong sim-to-real gains suggest practical value for robot learning pipelines that must bootstrap from limited offline data. RankQ learns relative action preferences rather than uniformly down-weighting unseen actions, directing action gradients toward higher-quality behaviors; it is evaluated on sparse-reward D4RL tasks and on offline-to-online fine-tuning of a pretrained vision-language-action model in both low-data and high-data regimes. In the high-data setting it improves simulation performance by 13.7 percentage points over the next best method.

## [ToolCUA Learns Optimal GUI-Tool Path Selection for Computer Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12481) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ToolCUA introduces an end-to-end agent that learns when to use atomic GUI actions versus high-level tool calls through a staged training paradigm, combining an Interleaved GUI-Tool Trajectory Scaling Pipeline, Tool-Bootstrapped GUI RFT, and Online Agentic RL with a Tool-Efficient Path Reward. On OSWorld-MCP it reaches 46.85% accuracy, a roughly 66% relative improvement over the baseline and a 3.9% gain over GUI-only settings, with code open-sourced at x-plug.github.io/ToolCUA. This addresses a core bottleneck in hybrid action spaces for computer use agents: deciding when to switch between GUI manipulation and API-based tools, which directly affects execution efficiency and reliability. The results suggest that training in a hybrid action space is a promising paradigm for real-world digital agents, potentially influencing how future autonomous agents are built and evaluated. The trajectory scaling pipeline repurposes abundant static GUI trajectories and uses MLLMs to synthesize a grounded tool library, avoiding costly real tool-trajectory collection; training then proceeds through warmup SFT plus single-turn RL, followed by online agentic RL in a high-fidelity GUI-Tool environment. The Tool-Efficient Path Reward explicitly encourages appropriate tool use and shorter execution paths, and the reported gains are on OSWorld-MCP among models of comparable scale.

ToolCUA tackles these problems with synthetic data scaling and staged reinforcement learning.

## [RoRo: Rubric-Guided Process Rewards for Stepwise Model Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29310) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.29310v2) proposes RoRo, a rubric-guided process reward framework for stepwise model routing in Large Reasoning Models. RoRo collects diverse routing trajectories, builds preference pairs based on outcome, cost, and process quality, then trains a Rubricor to generate query-specific rubrics and a Judge to score trajectories, combining these process rewards with outcome rewards to optimize the routing policy via GRPO. Existing stepwise routing methods model routing as a sequential process but still supervise routers only with outcome rewards, which reflect final answer correctness and ignore intermediate decision quality. By rewarding good intermediate routing decisions, RoRo could improve both accuracy and cost trade-offs of Large Reasoning Model inference, benefiting researchers and practitioners working on efficient reasoning deployment. RoRo uses alternating optimization to train the Rubricor and Judge, and its process rewards are combined with outcome rewards to optimize the routing policy via GRPO. Experiments on five reasoning benchmarks under both same-family and cross-family settings show consistent improvements over strong baselines, though the work remains an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion.

**Background**: Large Reasoning Models solve problems by generating long chains of intermediate reasoning steps, and stepwise model routing assigns each step to a suitable model to save compute. Process reward models score intermediate steps rather than only final answers, and GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm used to train such policies. Rubric-guided evaluation uses explicit, query-specific criteria to make LLM judgments more consistent and interpretable.

## [RedKnot: Head-Aware KV Cache Management for Long-Context LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06256) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RedKnot introduces a head-aware KV cache management system that decomposes the KV cache along KV heads instead of treating it as a monolithic token-level block sequence, and pairs it with SegPagedAttention, a per-head page table over a segmented KV store. The system uniformly supports position-independent KV reuse, prefix KV compression, hot/cold KV separation, and distributed KV placement without retraining or fine-tuning the model. As LLM input lengths grow, the KV cache has become the dominant bottleneck limiting GPU memory capacity, serving concurrency, cache reuse, and distributed scalability, so a more structured cache abstraction could substantially improve long-context serving efficiency. Because RedKnot requires no model retraining, it could be adopted by existing serving stacks and influence how future AI infrastructure manages memory. RedKnot exploits the observation that KV cache utility is highly structured across heads, with different heads having distinct functional roles, attention distances, and runtime importance, so a full KV cache is not always needed for every head, token range, or serving scenario. SegPagedAttention is especially useful for position-independent KV reuse, since when a cached chunk is reused after a new prefix, only prefix-sensitive global heads are recomputed with full-range attention while most local heads reuse cached KV states or access bounded visible regions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: In transformer-based LLMs, the KV cache stores the key and value tensors computed for previously processed tokens so they do not need to be recomputed at each decoding step, but its memory footprint grows linearly with sequence length. Existing serving systems typically manage this cache as a homogeneous sequence of token-level blocks with similar policies across all attention heads and scenarios. RedKnot instead treats the cache as a structured, model-aware memory object by decomposing it along KV heads, whose importance and effective attention ranges vary significantly across serving scenarios.

## [TARL Brings Five-Action Transactional Memory Updates to Long-Term Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03699) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2608.03699v4) introduces TARL, a transaction-aware memory update framework that maps each incoming statement to one of five executable actions — add, ignore, revise, reject, or defer — instead of the binary Write/Hold decision used by most existing agent memory systems. The authors also release TARL-Mem, a benchmark with fine-grained action labels and next-state targets, and train the model by comparing the memory states produced by alternative update operations. Long-term agents accumulate persistent memory, and a single bad update can repeatedly distort future retrieval and reasoning, so distinguishing whether information should be added, ignored, revised, rejected, or deferred is a meaningful step beyond binary memory gating. If the approach generalizes, it could reduce memory pollution and cumulative corruption in production agent systems that rely on long-lived knowledge stores. TARL identifies the affected memory, resolves its temporal scope, compares source reliability, and maintains accepted, pending, and rejected ledgers; it is trained by comparing memory states produced by alternative update operations to encourage selection of the operation yielding the correct result. Evaluations span in-domain, cross-source, temporal, counterfactual, and sequential settings, showing improved action prediction and state recovery, reduced memory pollution, preserved conflicting evidence, and limited cumulative corruption.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Long-term agents are AI systems that persist information across sessions so they can recall facts, preferences, or prior events later. Most current memory pipelines treat each new statement as a simple Write or Hold decision, which conflates very different situations — for example, a genuinely new fact versus a correction of an outdated belief versus an unreliable claim that should be deferred. TARL reframes this as a transaction-like update problem with multiple possible actions and separate ledgers for accepted, pending, and rejected information, borrowing the idea of a ledger from accounting and database systems.

It compares three revision settings — original venue reviews, AI-generated reviews, and fixed-prompt self-revision — and resolves 128 of 150 execution-related weaknesses (85.3%) but only 2 of 18 idea-related weaknesses (11.1%). This work shifts the evaluation of automated reviewing from review quality alone to measurable paper improvement, potentially reshaping how AI is used in peer review and scientific writing. It also reveals a key limitation: iterative AI revision can fix experiments and implementation but rarely addresses concerns about novelty or significance. The AI scientist has access to its previous versions during revision to mirror how human authors build on earlier drafts, while each review is generated independently with no memory of earlier feedback or scores to avoid bias. The human-initialized revisions are also assessed using Stanford Reviewer as an independent evaluator, and reviewer-guided revision consistently outperforms fixed-prompt self-revision.

## [Cognitive Field Networks Enable Persistent, Non-Episodic AI Cognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16752) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces the Cognitive Field Network (CFN), a recurrent Transformer in which an organized hidden field re-enters subsequent inference via the update rule Φ_{n+1} = F_θ(X_{n+1}, Φ_n), rather than relying on an explicitly prescribed memory operation. The authors report that learned recurrent timescales grow systematically with the trained recurrent horizon, and that semantic continuation propagates the recurrent state far beyond that horizon without replaying the target answer. Most current AI systems are episodic: they process each input independently and lack a persistent internal state that carries context across interactions. If CFN's history-dependent collective dynamics prove scalable, it could offer a controlled platform for building models with genuinely persistent cognition, affecting research directions in long-context reasoning, memory-augmented architectures, and cognitive science-inspired AI. The paper distinguishes three dynamical processes: collective memory dressing forms and sustains a history-dependent cognitive field, structured input reorganizes this field, and cross-cycle re-entry makes the resulting state causally available to later inference. Controls show that without content-specific support the field undergoes finite passive relaxation, while periodic re-exposure to relevant input renews the surviving state toward an approximately stationary nonzero regime; unrelated-input and recurrence-off controls do not reproduce this, and near-paraphrased re-exposure yields weaker renewal, indicating representation-sensitive persistence.

**Background**: Cognitive Field Theory (CFT) proposes that cognition arises from memory-dressed collective dynamics that generate a persistent macroscopic cognitive field, drawing on ideas from Gestalt cognitive field theory and more recent mathematical formulations treating knowledge as fields in a high-dimensional semantic space. Recurrent Transformers integrate explicit recurrence into standard Transformer modules, allowing iterative refinement of representations at the cost of some parallelism. CFN combines these threads by letting a recurrent Transformer maintain a persistent field instead of using a separately prescribed memory system.

## [Paper Proves Fundamental Limits of Confidence-Based Discrete Diffusion Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20581) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.20581v2) proves that discrete diffusion samplers, including remasking and uniform-state samplers, can only match the training distribution when the positions written in a step are conditionally independent given already-fixed tokens. It further shows that no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and that per-position marginals cannot determine whether a group is dependent. On the synthetic ScanAndAdd task, every group of two or more undetermined positions written by a confidence ranking is dependent, and the generated distribution measures 29× the sampling-noise floor in total variation while per-sample metrics remain 1.0. This theoretical result exposes a fundamental limitation in how discrete diffusion models are sampled, suggesting that confidence-based parallel sampling strategies may systematically fail to reproduce the true joint distribution of dependent tokens such as words, phonemes, or pixels. It could influence future model design and sampling strategies, pushing researchers toward methods that explicitly model inter-token dependencies rather than relying on per-position marginals. The paper establishes three formal results: a step matches the training distribution only when written positions are conditionally independent given fixed tokens; no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group; and two joint distributions can share identical per-position marginals while differing in which value combinations occur. The ScanAndAdd experiment provides a closed-form joint distribution for verification, showing a large total-variation gap (29× the noise floor) even though per-sample metrics look perfect at 1.0.

**Background**: Discrete diffusion models are a class of generative models that generate discrete data (such as text tokens) by iteratively denoising a corrupted sequence, and they are often proposed as an alternative to autoregressive language modeling. ## [Decoding Order Matters in Autoregressive Speech Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08450) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2601.08450v2) investigates decoding order in autoregressive speech synthesis using a masked diffusion framework, finding that fixed left-to-right decoding is suboptimal compared to adaptive strategies like Top-K. The study also shows that even 1-bit quantization of acoustic representations can support reasonably high-quality speech. This challenges the long-standing default of left-to-right generation in autoregressive speech synthesis, suggesting that rethinking decoding order and aggressive quantization could lead to more efficient and higher-quality speech generation models. The findings may influence future TTS system design and compression techniques. The masked diffusion framework allows arbitrary decoding orders during training and inference by progressively unmasking positions; the authors interpolate between identity and random permutations to show that randomness in decoding order affects speech quality. Fixed strategies like l2r and r2l are compared with adaptive ones such as Top-K, and 1-bit quantization is tested on discrete acoustic representations.

Researchers introduced HybridFlow, a three-stage generative policy inference procedure that requires only two network function evaluations (2-NFE) for robotic manipulation. It combines a Global Jump using MeanFlow average velocity, a parameter-free ReNoise interpolation to construct an intermediate state, and a Local Refine step querying the instantaneous-velocity limit of the same network, achieving 95% average success on RoboMimic ablations versus 78% for one-step MeanFlow. Across five real-robot settings with all policies running on the same Jetson AGX Thor, HybridFlow improved normalized task performance over 16-step Diffusion Policy by 13-68 points with approximately eightfold lower action-generation latency. The construction reuses a unified model without distillation, and additional experiments show compatibility as an action expert in a vision-language-action framework.

## [SOTAlign Aligns Vision and Language Models with Minimal Paired Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23353) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced SOTAlign, a two-stage semi-supervised framework that aligns frozen pretrained unimodal vision and language encoders using only a small number of image-text pairs plus large amounts of unpaired data. It first recovers a coarse shared geometry from limited paired data via a linear teacher, then refines alignment on unpaired samples using an optimal-transport-based divergence, significantly outperforming supervised and semi-supervised baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/SOTAlign. This work addresses a key bottleneck in multimodal learning: existing alignment methods typically require millions of paired image-text samples and contrastive losses. By drastically reducing the need for paired supervision, SOTAlign could make vision-language alignment more practical for domains where paired data is scarce or expensive to collect. SOTAlign uses a linear teacher to recover coarse shared geometry from limited paired data, then applies an optimal-transport-based divergence on unpaired samples to transfer relational structure without overconstraining the target space. It learns robust joint embeddings across datasets and encoder pairs, though as a preprint it has not yet undergone peer review or community validation.

## [Scaling Laws of SignSGD in Linear Regression: When Does It Outperform SGD?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02069) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper derives scaling laws for signSGD under a power-law random features (PLRF) model that accounts for both feature and target decay, analyzing the population risk of a linear model trained with one-pass signSGD on Gaussian-sketched features. It identifies a drift-normalization effect and a noise-reshaping effect unique to signSGD, and shows that the noise-reshaping effect can make the compute-optimal slope of signSGD steeper than that of SGD when noise is dominant. This provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for understanding when signSGD, a core component of adaptive optimizers like Adam, can outperform standard SGD in terms of compute-optimal scaling. It could inform the design of more efficient training algorithms for large-scale machine learning models. The analysis expresses risk as a function of model size, training steps, learning rate, and feature and target decay parameters, and compares it against the SGD risk analyzed by Paquette et al. (2024). It further shows that the warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedule reduces the noise term and sharpens the compute-optimal slope when feature decay is fast but target decay is slow.

Researchers introduced C2C, an object-centric cognition-to-control architecture that standardizes the physical semantics exchanged between HRC modules via 'physical contracts' rather than standardizing the modules themselves. By making key components plug-compatible without redefining the collaboration task, C2C could significantly lower integration costs and accelerate deployment of humanoid robots in real-world collaborative transport and manufacturing settings. The contracts represent task intent as a geometrically verified payload path, partner information as a source-independent physical state, and learned coordination as bounded 11-D task-space commands, while robot-specific feasibility stays inside whole-body control. The same interfaces support neural and interpretable hard-tree actors, two- and three-carrier teams, and simulated-to-human partner substitution, with a three-carrier system of two G1 humanoids and one human validating the structure on hardware.

## [Dial: A Knowledge-Grounded Framework for Dialect-Specific NL2SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.07449) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present Dial, a knowledge-grounded framework for dialect-specific NL2SQL that converts natural language into SQL queries executable on different database engines. Dial combines a Dialect-Aware Logical Query Planning module, a hierarchical intent-aware knowledge base called HINT-KB, and an execution-driven debugging and semantic verification loop, and it introduces DS-NL2SQL, a benchmark covering six major database systems with 2,218 dialect-specific test cases. Experiments report a 10.25% improvement in translation accuracy and a 15.77% gain in dialect feature coverage over state-of-the-art baselines. Most existing NL2SQL methods assume a single canonical dialect such as SQLite, so they often fail to produce queries that are both semantically correct and executable on real enterprise engines. By explicitly modeling dialect differences, Dial addresses a practical gap for enterprises running heterogeneous database systems and could improve how natural-language interfaces, AI agents, and analytics tools interact with production databases. Dial decomposes intent at the operator level and performs divergence-aware specification to build a dialect-aware logical query plan, while HINT-KB organizes dialect knowledge into a Canonical Syntax Reference, a declarative function repository, and a procedural constraint repository. Its verification loop separates syntactic recovery from logic auditing to prevent semantic drift, and the DS-NL2SQL benchmark spans six major database systems with 2,218 dialect-specific test cases.
