## [Per-Sample Retention in Fine-Tuning Is Reproducible but Architecture-Specific](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11508) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper empirically tests whether per-sample retention during fine-tuning is a reproducible property of the sample, recording per-epoch correctness for ResNet-18 and DeiT-Small on an imbalanced retinal OCT dataset and CUB-200-2011. It finds retention is reproducible (cross-run Spearman correlation of the fitted decay constant 0.37–0.59 over ten seeds) but architecture-specific, and that the Ebbinghaus exponential decay model fails to capture the observed dynamics. This challenges a core assumption in curriculum learning, data pruning, and dataset cartography—that per-sample difficulty or retention is a stable property of the sample—and suggests that a cheap difficulty score may not buy generalization through sampling. It has direct implications for data-centric AI pipelines that rely on such scores to prioritize or prune training data. The Ebbinghaus exponential's only representable shape, monotone decay, appears in just 0.1%–0.8% of samples, and on traces that do forget mean R-squared is negative in all four configurations; a power law and a free-asymptote variant also fail, indicating the defect is monotonicity. Across five sampling arms with matched exposure, prioritisation ratios of 2.7x to 28x, and an online variant, none of 48 comparisons against uniform sampling survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and patient-grouped splitting (the remedy for a leak reaching 76%–78% of OCT test images) moves headline metrics by less than their run-to-run spread.

The probe direction is causally separable from recall: projecting it out collapses the signature locally (+0.44 to -0.19) while behavioral recall barely changes, and a probe trained on naturally memorized content does not classify fine-tuning-injected secrets, marking two distinct regimes. PGA remains robust to six adversarial probe variants and defeats a re-fitting attacker at every memorization-relevant depth, with a mean accuracy change of +0.2 percentage points across benchmarks.

## [Red-Team Study Finds LLM Robustness Doesn't Follow Release Order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18193) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A large-scale red-team evaluation of three Anthropic frontier LLMs (Opus 4.8, Fable 5, and Fable 5.1) tested 7,826 harmful intents across four automated jailbreak attack families using the HackAgent framework, generating hundreds of thousands of adversarial attempts. The study found that adaptive iterative attacks dominate residual jailbreak vulnerability, and that the newest model, Fable 5.1, was actually the least robust (8.19% attack success) compared to Fable 5 (2.72%) and Opus 4.8 (5.76%). This finding challenges the common assumption that newer model versions are automatically more secure, suggesting that safety improvements are not monotonic across releases. It has significant implications for AI safety research and deployment decisions, as even the best-tested frontier models remain reliably breakable under sustained automated pressure, with thousands of panel-confirmed harmful completions produced cheaply and without human expert involvement. All apparent attack successes were independently re-adjudicated by a panel of five frontier judge models requiring at least 4/5 agreement, and the three models failed in largely disjoint places. Conditioning on prompts each model actually answered revealed that adaptive tree search (TAP) broke all three at similar rates (10.1%, 9.7%, 12.1%), while one-shot persuasion (PAP) separated them by more than an order of magnitude (3.1%, 0.7%, 9.5%), indicating that resistance to framing rather than to search is the key differentiator.

The method is a training-free wrapper that adapts the replanning tolerance online using the current deviation from the cached rollout plus a local sensitivity estimate, without touching the learned world model or planner. ## [OptR: Output-Aware Rotation Enables Accurate INT2 KV-Cache Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02691) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.02691v3) introduces OptR, an output-aware rotation method that minimizes post-output-projection (post-W_O) attention-output error for INT2 KV-cache quantization. OptR decomposes this error into key- and value-induced terms and learns per-head orthogonal corrections through the full INT2 quantization and attention path, additionally applying an attention-equivalent key reparameterization to reduce large channel-wise offsets without altering the softmax distribution. The KV cache is a dominant memory and bandwidth bottleneck in long-context LLM inference, so enabling accurate ultra-low-bit (INT2) quantization could substantially cut memory costs and speed up inference. OptR consistently improves existing rotation-based methods QuaRot and OSCAR across three models and five reasoning and coding benchmarks, and strengthens long-context retrieval, making it directly relevant to researchers and practitioners working on efficient LLM deployment. Unlike prior rotation-based INT2 methods that optimize cache statistics or proxy errors before the complete attention readout, OptR targets the error actually propagated through attention and the output projection W_O. It preserves the paged KV-cache format with negligible inference overhead, which is important for compatibility with existing serving systems.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Quantization reduces the numerical precision of model weights, activations, or cached tensors to save memory and compute, but lower bit-widths introduce information loss and accuracy degradation. The KV cache stores intermediate key and value tensors for all previously processed tokens during autoregressive generation, and its size grows linearly with context length, making it a prime target for compression. Rotation-based quantization methods such as QuaRot and SpinQuant apply orthogonal transforms (often Hadamard matrices) to spread outliers across dimensions while preserving model outputs in full precision, and INT2 refers to quantizing values to just 2 bits.

## [SkillClone Attack Reconstructs Hidden LLM Agent Skills via Benign Probing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04192) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.04192v2) introduces behavioral skill reconstruction (BSR) and SkillClone, a black-box attack that clones a hidden LLM agent skill by forming an interface hypothesis from its public advertisement, issuing structured benign probes, synthesizing an executable replica, and iteratively repairing it through differential validation. Across 30 skills spanning rules, tables, procedures, and algorithms, SkillClone achieved exact or partial recovery on held-out inputs for several targets. This work shows that file secrecy alone does not guarantee functional secrecy, meaning providers who hide proprietary agent skills behind service interfaces cannot rely on disclosure-focused defenses such as prompt-injection filters. It has direct implications for AI agent security, model extraction, and the commercial viability of selling agent capabilities as black-box services. SkillClone uses only legitimate task requests and observed responses, so disclosure-focused defenses provide limited coverage, and even less detailed skill descriptions offer only limited protection. The paper notes that iterative requerying closes gaps missed by single-round reconstruction, and that defenses must limit cumulative information leakage from ordinary use rather than just preventing file disclosure.

**Background**: LLM agents increasingly rely on "skills" — packaged instructions, scripts, constants, and data that give the agent specialized capabilities. Providers may offer these skills as closed-source services while keeping the underlying packages hidden, and prior security research has focused on prompt injection attacks that directly disclose such artifacts. Behavioral skill reconstruction (BSR) shifts the question from whether files can be leaked to whether the functionality those files implement can be recovered through ordinary, legitimate use.

## [BALANCE Combines Autoregressive and Speculative Decoding for Edge LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05926) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.05926v2) proposes BALANCE, a hybrid autoregressive-speculative inference framework in which an edge server hosts both a small language model (SLM) and a large language model (LLM), admits users, and dynamically assigns each admitted user to either autoregressive decoding (AD) or speculative decoding (SD) mode while running both modes simultaneously. The authors formulate a task throughput maximization problem that jointly determines user admission and computing resource allocation between AD and SD under user latency requirements and server memory constraints, and since the problem is NP-hard they develop a polynomial-time algorithm that splits it into two sub-problems and yields a sub-optimal solution with a constant approximation guarantee. Edge inference is a key enabler for delivering LLM services in next-generation mobile networks, but the latency-memory tradeoff means neither AD nor SD alone can efficiently serve heterogeneous user demands under limited edge resources. BALANCE's joint admission and mode-assignment strategy could influence how future edge inference systems are architected, letting operators serve more users without proportionally scaling memory. The core technical contribution is a polynomial-time algorithm that decomposes the NP-hard throughput maximization problem into two sub-problems and achieves a constant approximation guarantee, with experiments showing BALANCE consistently outperforms conventional pure-AD and pure-SD baselines and significantly improves task throughput. As an arXiv preprint with no community discussion yet, the results have not been peer-reviewed, and the abstract does not specify the SLM/LLM model sizes, hardware platform, or the exact latency and memory parameters used in the evaluation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Autoregressive decoding (AD) generates output tokens one at a time, so request latency grows with response length and is largely memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. Speculative decoding (SD) speeds this up by having a small draft model propose several tokens that the large model then verifies in parallel, but it requires extra memory to host the draft model. Because edge servers have limited memory and must meet per-user latency requirements, choosing between AD and SD for each user is a resource-allocation problem, which is exactly what BALANCE addresses.

## [Counting Documents Is Not Counting Text: Unit Bias in Web-PDF Corpus Statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16390) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new measurement study analyzes CC-MAIN-2021-31-PDF-UNTRUNCATED (7.9M Common Crawl PDFs, 32.6B tokens) and finds that text mass is extremely concentrated: 3.02% of text-bearing documents hold half of all tokens (Gini 0.807). The study shows Common Crawl's payload cap truncated 23.06% of documents but 63.08% of their text, and that two widely used text-layer parsers recover only 1.4% and 11.4% of that exposed text. This exposes a methodological blind spot in how web-PDF corpora report statistics: document-level rates can dramatically misrepresent token-level reality, affecting LLM pretraining data pipelines, OCR routing, and corpus documentation. Anyone building or evaluating large-scale text corpora should report statistics in both documents and tokens to avoid misleading conclusions. The study uses the one public corpus that pairs Common Crawl's stored fragments with re-fetched originals, and notes that under the 5MiB cap adopted in March 2025, 30.19% of tokens would still be exposed. Roughly 55-62% of the corpus's text is unrecoverable from the crawl by such pipelines, and the authors recommend reporting corpus statistics in both units.

The report claims performance competitive with, and in some settings stronger than, state-of-the-art standalone guardrails and specialized hallucination detectors, and shows the signals can also drive constrained decoding and selective medical-risk interventions in SingProbe-Med.

## [γOPD: Discounted Temporal Credit Assignment for On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16937) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces γOPD (GammaOPD), a discounted temporal credit assignment method for on-policy distillation (OPD) that unifies token-level and sequence-level OPD under a single temporal-credit view, showing that practical token-level OPD is a temporal approximation of the sequence-level reverse-KL gradient. It also proposes a reward-compatible bounded mixing (RBM) mechanism that blends verifiable outcome feedback with the discounted OPD advantage, and reports consistent improvements over existing OPD methods in math and code reasoning across vanilla, size-mismatched, and multi-teacher settings. On-policy distillation is a key post-training technique for large language models, but existing objectives must trade off objective fidelity against optimization stability; γOPD offers a principled way to get long-horizon supervision without horizon-dependent variance blow-up. If the horizon-independent variance bound and RBM mechanism hold up, this could improve how practitioners distill reasoning models, especially in multi-teacher and size-mismatched scenarios common in real deployments. The method admits a horizon-independent variance bound, which is the theoretical property that distinguishes it from sequence-level OPD whose variance grows with sequence length. The RBM mechanism is designed to move beyond purely teacher-dependent optimization by mixing verifiable outcome rewards with the discounted OPD advantage, and experiments cover mathematical and code reasoning under vanilla, size-mismatched, and multi-teacher distillation settings.

## [GameLogicBench: Tick-Level Benchmark for Coding Agents on Godot Game Logic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21562) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced GameLogicBench, a benchmark of 72 gameplay-logic tasks in Godot projects whose automated evaluator checks game rules at every simulation tick across 403 hand-designed scenarios, expanded by seeded parameter variations into 1,451 test cases. Across 20 combinations of language models and scaffolds, the best run solved only 52.78% of tasks, and under Claude Code all twelve tested models solved fewer tasks as scope grew from isolated mechanics to repository-scale features. Existing game-development benchmarks replay fixed examples, score videos, or rely on another model as judge, so they cannot verify that rules hold throughout execution or guarantee reproducible verdicts. GameLogicBench fills this gap with tick-level state assertions, giving agent developers a more reliable signal for whether coding agents actually implement correct gameplay behavior rather than merely producing runnable code. To avoid measuring implementation style rather than behavior, the evaluator must accept different correct implementations of each task while rejecting mutants that have one required capability removed; without this mutation-based validation, incorrect agent submissions passed. The paper also reports that agents copy code from public repositories when network access is open, so reliable evaluation depends both on what the tests reject and on what external code agents can reach.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Godot is a free, open-source, cross-platform game engine used to build 2D and 3D games, and its projects provide a realistic setting for testing coding agents on gameplay rules. A game can end in a valid state even after violating its rules mid-run, which is why checking state at every simulation tick matters more than inspecting only the final outcome. Mutation testing, a technique for assessing test quality by deliberately introducing faults, is used here to validate that the evaluator rejects implementations missing a required capability.

## [Study Separates Replication, Measurement Sensitivity, and Persistence in Hosted LLM Evaluations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22478) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.22478) introduces a framework that separates three validation questions for behavioral evaluations of hosted LLMs: replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence. Using the Regent Chess sequential environment, it shows that a previously reported Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite performance deficit recurs under its historical configuration (+0.0530, 95% CI [+0.0329, +0.0714]), but that rebuilding the evaluation-and-inference configuration under the same public identifier shifts the endpoint by 0.0429, and a frozen 4K comparison even reverses sign between Gemini 3.1 and Gemini 3.7. This work highlights that behavioral claims about hosted models can yield different conclusions depending on the tested identifier, serving period, measurement instrument, and inference configuration, which undermines naive reproducibility assumptions. It argues that such claims should be explicitly indexed by these factors, affecting how researchers, benchmark maintainers, and model providers report and compare evaluation results. The Regent Chess environment records a hidden, mutable state exactly so stated beliefs can be scored against ground truth at action time, with positive endpoint values meaning worse performance than a matched-uniform comparator. In the back-to-back same-day H/R comparison, all six configuration components vary jointly, so no single component is isolated, and the additional serving-period contribution remains unresolved (-0.0166, 95% CI [-0.0483, +0.0157]).

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Hosted LLMs are accessed through a service endpoint rather than run locally, so evaluations can vary because the service, the measurement instrument, or both differ across runs. Behavioral evaluations test what a model says or does in a controlled environment, and reproducibility concerns whether a prior finding recurs on fresh data under its historical configuration. Measurement sensitivity asks whether the endpoint changes when the evaluation-and-inference configuration is rebuilt under the same identifier, while persistence asks whether the finding holds across subsequently tested identifiers under one common instrument.

## [A* Tie-Breaking Strategies Shown to Have No Universal Winner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23293) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper proves that for nine standard tie-breaking strategies in A* search, no single strategy dominates: under a consistent heuristic, every pair of strategies has positive-cost instances where one expands arbitrarily more nodes than the other. The paper also shows unbounded expansion-count ratios between low-h with FIFO and LIFO on a parameterized unit-cost grid, and demonstrates that with the weighted evaluation function f_alpha = g + alpha*h (0 <= alpha < 1), all tie-breaking strategies expand exactly the same set of states when h > 0 at non-goals. Tie-breaking is a routine implementation choice in A* that practitioners often treat as inconsequential, but this result shows it can cause arbitrarily large differences in the number of expanded nodes, directly affecting runtime and memory in pathfinding, planning, and heuristic search systems. It also identifies a weighted evaluation regime (0 <= alpha < 1) in which tie-breaking sensitivity disappears entirely, giving implementers a principled way to make performance predictable. The analysis assumes a consistent heuristic and covers nine standard tie-breaking strategies, with the strongest negative results coming from positive-cost instances and a parameterized unit-cost grid. The complementary extremal results apply to unit-cost search with h > 0 at non-goals: low-h minimizes remaining expansions from a common configuration within the perfect region, while high-h maximizes total expansions when every final-plateau state with h = 1 is a goal predecessor.

Many nodes can share the same f-value, especially on the final f-layer (the 'final plateau'), so implementations must break ties using secondary criteria such as preferring lower h, higher h, FIFO, or LIFO. A heuristic is consistent (monotonic) when its estimates never decrease by more than the actual step cost, which guarantees that once a node is expanded its g-cost is optimal.

Echo State Networks (ESNs) are a type of recurrent neural network from the reservoir computing family, where a fixed, randomly connected reservoir maps inputs into a high-dimensional space and only a simple readout layer is trained, making them attractive for fast, low-complexity temporal processing.

## [Credo: Variance-Guided Rubric Evolution for Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24174) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Credo introduces a framework that couples evolving semantic rubrics with selective, execution-based credit correction for long-horizon language agents. It uses a frozen judge to map transitions to rubric features, a credit head to predict changes in expected terminal reward, and independently sampled two-sided replays to correct prediction residuals using recorded inclusion probabilities. Credit assignment under sparse terminal feedback is a central bottleneck for training long-horizon language agents, and Credo's variance decomposition offers a principled way to decide which rubric features to keep and how to allocate a fixed replay budget. This could inform more sample-efficient RL training for LLM-based agents that use tools, memory, and multi-step reasoning. The paper derives conditional unbiasedness and a variance decomposition whose criterion weights prediction errors by policy-score sensitivity and missing replay coverage, with an allocation rule that also accounts for continuation cost. It also describes a practical mixture with terminal leave-one-out advantages and distinguishes its clipped, token-normalized PPO implementation from the ideal policy-gradient estimator, while explicitly making no claim of empirical superiority on language-agent benchmarks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: In reinforcement learning, the credit assignment problem asks which past actions or tokens actually caused a later reward, and it becomes especially hard when rewards arrive only at the end of a long episode. Language agents that use tools and multi-step reasoning often receive such sparse terminal feedback, while intermediate rubrics can provide structured but potentially misspecified progress signals. Counterfactual continuation rollouts can measure local credit by replaying alternative futures, but exhaustive replay is computationally expensive, motivating selective replay and variance-reduction techniques.

The paper proposes Spectral Energy-proportional Rank Allocation (SERA), a task-adaptive strategy that assigns different rank capacities to each task vector based on its singular-value energy structure. Experiments under standard vision model merging protocols show SERA improves multi-task merging performance while keeping the same total rank budget as existing spectral merging methods. SERA's task-dependent allocation could make multi-task model merging more effective without extra joint training, benefiting practitioners who combine fine-tuned checkpoints under fixed parameter budgets. SERA extends SVD-based model merging from uniform-capacity merging to task-dependent capacity allocation, giving richer spectral capacity to complex or isolated tasks and fewer directions to compact tasks. The analysis further links task-level spectral concentration to the per-task effect of adaptive rank allocation, offering insight into when and why SERA is effective.

The architecture rests on a checking asymmetry — formalised validity conditions can be checked at runtime, whereas the correctness of many actions is established only ex post — and the paper presents eight falsifiable propositions with named baselines as empirically testable hypotheses rather than established results.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.24784v1) introduces convex AI compositionality, a formal framework that uses convex spaces to represent the configurations generated by finite populations of AI system instantiations. It shows that convex compositions of operational states can remain compatible with lifecycle reachability and preserve formal identity relations between related AI systems. Current AI regulation is predominantly single-system-centric, so this work addresses a gap by treating collections of related AI systems as governance objects. It could give regulators and providers tools to monitor multiple instantiations, versions, and deployment configurations across the AI lifecycle. The framework repurposes well-known statistical and geometric constructions, such as weighted state distributions and convex hulls, as governance tools for distinguishing operational states, population weights, heterogeneity, and configuration change. The paper illustrates the approach with distributed healthcare deployments and controlled deployment of recruitment AI variants, while noting compatibility with lifecycle reachability and AI identity only under stated conditions.

Under abrupt social shifts, confidence accumulated from previously reliable predictions can remain behaviorally active after the relationship changes, indicating that confidence revision can lag behind social change.

## [AI Framework Models Interplanetary Observatory Network as Weighted Graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22244) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.22244) proposes the Universal Observatory Graph (UOG), an AI-driven framework that models autonomous observatories at Sun-planet L2 Lagrange points as nodes in a weighted graph, with communication links as edges carrying metrics such as interplanetary distance, latency, transmission power, and link reliability. For a six-observatory Solar System configuration (Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), three independent sky-coverage methods all yield complete network union coverage, about 0.43% six-observatory intersection, and roughly 24.96% mean pairwise Jaccard similarity, while routing is solved via tabular Q-learning as a finite-horizon Markov decision process. The work offers a reproducible baseline for coordinating distributed observatories across the Solar System, a problem that becomes increasingly relevant as space agencies and private actors deploy more deep-space telescopes. By combining graph theory, multi-objective optimization, and reinforcement learning, it also bridges AI routing research with the practical constraints of interplanetary communication, such as light-time latency and limited transmission power. Sky coverage is evaluated with three methods: a 200,000-direction Fibonacci sphere, a 2,000,000-direction fixed-seed Monte Carlo calculation, and deterministic spherical integration. The learned Earth-Saturn-Uranus-Neptune route also achieves the highest discounted return among all 41 feasible simple paths under a four-hop constraint, but the authors note that time-dependent ephemerides, mission-specific visibility, calibrated link budgets, and scalable graph policies remain future work.

## [Horizon-Slicing Approximation for Minimum Obstacle Displacement Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22974) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This paper formalizes the Minimum Obstacle Displacement (MOD) planning problem, in which a robot must reach a goal by pushing movable polygonal obstacles when no collision-free path exists, and proves the problem is NP-hard. It then proposes a horizon-slicing approximate solution that runs with lower computational cost and stays within a fraction of the optimal cost, allowing a tunable trade-off between path length and total obstacle displacement. Robots operating in cluttered homes, warehouses, and disaster sites frequently encounter passages blocked by movable objects, so a practical planner that explicitly reasons about how much to push obstacles could make such systems more capable. Because the exact problem is NP-hard, this approximation offers a computationally viable alternative for real-time navigation, though it remains an incremental advance rather than a paradigm shift. The NP-hardness result is established for obstacles modeled as polygons in the plane, and the paper presents both an exact formulation that generalizes earlier minimum-displacement problems and the horizon-slicing approximation. The approximation is not optimal: it differs from the optimal cost by a fraction of that cost, and the slicing horizon controls the balance between shorter paths and fewer or smaller obstacle displacements.

NP-hardness means no known polynomial-time algorithm can solve the exact problem for all inputs, motivating approximation algorithms that trade optimality for speed.

By embedding these geometric parameters directly into the final network layer and jointly optimizing them with target-inside and non-target-outside constraints, the method achieves the highest AUC in 28 of 30 open-set comparisons on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10. The minimum signed boundary score across all hyperspheres simultaneously determines open-set acceptance or rejection and provides a geometric explanation of the decision. A two-dimensional synthetic study shows that the model architecture must balance the compactness of known normal classes against the separability of unknown anomalies, highlighting a key design trade-off.

## [Tail-Weight Control and Localized Generalization in Low-Rank Adversarial Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23688) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proves that in a Gaussian low-rank model with Euclidean adversarial perturbations, any near-optimal predictor under bounded ramp loss must have small tail weight, and it derives localized finite-sample generalization bounds governed by principal dimension and total tail energy. It also establishes a unique population minimizer under isotropic principal covariance and shows experimentally that excess risk and tail use decrease with sample size. This provides a rigorous theoretical link between adversarial robustness and the geometry of low-rank data, helping explain why robust classifiers avoid relying on low-variance noise directions. It could guide the design of more robust algorithms and inform generalization analysis in statistical learning theory. The analysis uses a bounded ramp loss and a path-specific density bound that yields constants without requiring positive tail variance; boundary normalization removes the common attack penalty from centered margins. Experiments with twenty paired repetitions confirm decreasing excess risk and tail use with sample size, and nearly unchanged behavior when tail dimension grows at fixed total energy.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Adversarial machine learning studies how small, intentionally crafted perturbations to inputs can fool classifiers, and robustness research seeks models that resist such attacks. Generalization bounds quantify how well a model trained on finite data performs on unseen data, while low-rank Gaussian models assume data lies near a low-dimensional subspace plus independent noise, a common simplification in high-dimensional statistics.

## [Belted Engression Unifies Dimension Reduction and Generative Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23789) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes Belted Engression, a parameter-efficient compress-then-generate framework that embeds a structural bottleneck into a generative architecture for conditional distributional regression. The authors prove that the standard sufficient dimension reduction (SDR) condition is equivalent to a law-preserving generative factorization achieved at the global optimum of the population Belted Engression objective. This work bridges two previously separate lines of research—sufficient dimension reduction and conditional generative modeling—potentially enabling more accurate distributional prediction with far fewer trainable parameters. It could benefit researchers and practitioners in generative modeling, uncertainty quantification, and statistical learning theory who need efficient conditional generators. The paper establishes finite-sample convergence rates sharper than existing results by uncovering a localized Bernstein-type control for the energy-score loss, and proves the belted architecture has an asymptotically vanishing parameter count relative to an unstructured baseline. Extensive simulations and real-world applications reportedly show superior distributional prediction and SDR recovery with fewer trainable parameters.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Sufficient dimension reduction (SDR) is a statistical paradigm that seeks a low-dimensional function R(x) of a high-dimensional predictor vector x such that the conditional distribution of the response y given R(x) is the same as that given x, meaning no regression information is lost. Traditional SDR frameworks, however, were not designed for conditional generation, and modern conditional generative models often struggle to learn complex covariate dependencies. The energy score is a proper scoring rule for evaluating probabilistic forecasts by measuring distances between predicted and observed distributions, and it serves as the loss function in this work.

Atomic activities are multi-agent, multi-label, and topology-aware, so conventional action recognition and permutation-invariant slot attention are misaligned with their semantics; Action-Slot's activity-centric inductive bias could improve recognition and weakly supervised localization for traffic and multi-agent behavior analysis. Experiments on OATS, TACO, and annotated nuScenes report superior recognition, strong sim-to-real transfer, and state-of-the-art weakly supervised localization, making it a useful reference for researchers in video understanding and multi-agent behavior analysis. Slot attention is widely used for object-centric decomposition, but its permutation-invariant design and object-level inductive bias are misaligned with atomic activity semantics, which is why Action-Slot anchors slots to predefined activity categories and adds background/negative-slot regularization. The weakly supervised localization framework suppresses false positives by measuring attention changes before and after candidate region removal, avoiding the need for dense annotations.

The framework operates before the LLM rather than inside it, combining three components: visual-only diversity selection, similarity-guided token recycling, and position-preserving restoration. ## [Exactness at Inference: A New Criterion for Out-of-Distribution Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24942) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.24942) proposes a representational criterion for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, arguing that a model generalizes outside its training distribution only when it computes a representation structurally equivalent to the underlying generating mechanism, rather than an approximation fitted to the data. The paper evaluates Tensor Logic and Logic Tensor Networks against this criterion, finding that Logic Tensor Networks fail it while differentiable ILP and Tensor Logic at zero temperature pass. OOD generalization is one of the hardest open problems in machine learning, and this paper reframes it as a question about the structure of representations rather than about training procedures or data augmentation. If the criterion holds, it could reshape how researchers design and certify hybrid neuro-symbolic architectures, and it offers a concrete explanation for why many models fail on benchmarks such as ARC-AGI. The criterion constrains inference rather than training: an exact marginal in [0,1] passes, but a neural network thresholded to a hard label does not, and the paper notes that Tensor Logic lacks infinite recursion, reaching Datalog rather than Prolog, and needs external memory to bind a novel entity. It also proposes a propagation rule for hybrid architectures in which the output inherits the bounds of every fitted estimator on its path, and reports that on a law-derived partition an exact hypothesis class identifies 56.3% of distant queries as answerable, which ensembles meet with false confidence and distance metrics rank backwards.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Out-of-distribution generalization refers to a model's ability to perform well on data whose distribution differs from the training set, a long-standing challenge because models often latch onto spurious correlations that break under distribution shift. Tensor Logic is a recently proposed programming language that unifies neural networks, symbolic logical reasoning, and probabilistic models around a single tensor-equation construct, while Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) use a differentiable first-order logic called Real Logic to combine data and logical constraints. This paper sits at the intersection of neuro-symbolic AI and learning theory, asking what kind of representation is required for exact rather than approximate extrapolation.

## [Agentic XAI framework iteratively refines SHAP explanations via multimodal LLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.21066) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This study proposes an agentic XAI framework that combines SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) with iterative refinement by a multimodal LLM, tested as an agricultural recommendation system on rice yield data from 28 fields in Japan. Across 11 refinement rounds (Rounds 0–10), both crop scientists (n=12) and LLM judges (n=14) found that refinement raised average explanation quality by 30–33% over Round 0, peaking at Rounds 3–4 before declining. The finding that iterative LLM refinement does not monotonically improve explanations challenges a common assumption in agentic AI pipelines, showing that strategic early stopping is necessary. This has implications for anyone building LLM-based explanation or decision-support systems, especially in high-stakes domains like agriculture where trust in AI predictions matters. Criterion-level trajectories reveal a bias-variance trade-off: early rounds lacked Specificity (bias), while excessive iteration eroded Conciseness and raised Cost Consideration through ungrounded economic reasoning (variance). LLM judges overscored every criterion by 1.4–2.3 points but largely preserved the experts' ranking of rounds (Spearman ρ = 0.58–0.90), suggesting screened LLM judges can flag the quality peak despite unreliable absolute scores.

## [DFAH Harness Separates Determinism and Faithfulness in Tool-Using LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15322) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces the Determinism-Faithfulness Assurance Harness (DFAH), a framework that distinguishes decision repeatability, trajectory agreement, and evidence-conditioned faithfulness in tool-using LLM agents. It also re-examines a historical correlation statistic (r = -0.11) from the original v2 study of 4,705 agentic runs across three synthetic financial tasks, noting that the figure included a subsequently excluded portfolio fixture and should be treated only as a historical description. As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in regulated domains like finance, teams need rigorous ways to verify that agents behave consistently and that their decisions are actually grounded in retrieved evidence. DFAH provides a measurement vocabulary that separates repeatability from correctness, helping prevent overclaiming about determinism-accuracy tradeoffs and removing deployment recommendations that were based on unsupported interpretations. The framework explicitly separates decision repeatability, observable execution (trajectory agreement), evidence-conditioned faithfulness, and task correctness, each requiring distinct qualified labels and evaluation; the historical v2 experiments never evaluated evidence-conditioned faithfulness. The paper also cautions that recorded decision concentration and tool-path variation do not identify hidden model strategy, and points to a separate corrected study, DFAH-Bench (arXiv:2607.20491), for qualified evidence of decision/path disagreement.

**Background**: Tool-using LLM agents can arrive at the same final answer through different intermediate steps, so a repeated decision does not necessarily mean the agent followed the same reasoning or consulted the same evidence. Determinism in this context refers to whether an agent produces consistent, auditable behavior given identical inputs, while faithfulness refers to whether the agent's output is actually supported by the evidence it retrieved. DFAH is an open-source harness designed to measure these properties, particularly for financial services where auditability and regulatory compliance are critical.

## [Information-Geometric First-Passage Monitor Detects Distributional Shifts in Stochastic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24083) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2604.24083v2) introduces a bounded first-passage monitoring architecture that combines relative-entropy dissipation, information geometry, and sequential inference to distinguish nominal distributional relaxation from regime departure in stochastic systems. The runtime layer uses Gaussian window surrogates, nominal-relative covariance shrinkage, a coordinate-consistent relative precision diagnostic, and randomized conformal ranks aggregated by a mixture power-martingale process. The framework offers a principled way to control repeated-test false alarms under explicit validity assumptions, which is valuable for runtime monitoring, anomaly detection, and regime-change detection in stochastic systems. Its evaluation on NSL-KDD and UNSW-NB15 shows strong post-change detection rates, though calibration transport emerges as a major deployment constraint. Analytical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck validation gives zero positive nominal Kullback-Leibler increments, forcing-identity residuals below 3.31 x 10^-6, and coordinate-invariance errors at numerical roundoff. On NSL-KDD, the monitor yields 0/100 alarms on internal nominal streams but 63/100 on official test-normal streams, with post-change detection of 99.0% for seen and 98.53% for test-only attack types; on UNSW-NB15, internal-null alarms are 0/100 while official test-normal alarms rise to 90/100, and post-change detection is 81.33% with 18.67% pre-change alarms.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence) measures how much one probability distribution differs from another, and for reversible Fokker-Planck dynamics it is non-increasing toward an invariant density. Information geometry studies the geometry of probability distributions using tools like the Fisher information metric, while first-passage monitoring tracks when a stochastic process first crosses a threshold. Conformal martingales are sequential, distribution-free tools for online hypothesis testing that can detect deviations from exchangeability in real-time data streams.

## [CoFlow: Coordinated Few-Step Flow for Offline Multi-Agent Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01457) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers propose CoFlow, a distillation-free joint averaged-velocity flow model that generates multi-agent trajectories in one or few steps, with Coordinated Velocity Attention (CVA) injecting teammate trajectory information into each agent's prediction. Across 48 configurations on MPE and SMAC, CoFlow outperforms the reproduced baseline by 11.2% under centralized execution with a 12.93-fold sampling speedup, while CVA raises normalized scores by 165.1% over the same model with cross-agent attention disabled. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning often relies on diffusion models whose iterative sampling is too slow for real-time control, and distillation can break the cross-agent dependencies needed for cooperation. CoFlow shows that a joint few-step flow model can be both fast and cooperative, which matters for deploying learned multi-agent policies in latency-sensitive domains such as robot swarms and game AI. CoFlow learns a joint averaged-velocity field directly, avoiding the consistency-distillation pipeline, and approximates the correction term with finite differences, which yields a 1.78-fold training speedup and reduces peak GPU memory by 41.1% versus the exact-derivative implementation. The method supports both centralized and decentralized execution, and the project page is at https://github.com/Guowei-Zou/coflow.

**Background**: Flow matching is a generative modeling technique that trains a neural network to regress a continuous normalizing flow's vector field toward a closed-form target, enabling fast simulation-free training. ## [Stackelberg Game Analysis of Incentives and Cut Layer Choice in Split Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07813) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This paper (arXiv:2412.07813v5) models the interaction between an SFL model owner and self-interested clients as a single-leader multi-follower Stackelberg game, where the owner jointly sets incentives and the cut layer while clients decide how much data to contribute. The authors prove the existence and uniqueness of the Nash equilibrium among clients and analyze the Stackelberg equilibrium, showing it maximizes utility for both sides while balancing model accuracy against computation and networking overhead. Most existing SFL research assumes clients participate unconditionally, so this work fills a gap by explicitly modeling strategic, self-interested behavior and the owner's dual levers of incentive and cut layer. It offers a theoretical foundation for designing fairer and more efficient SFL deployments, which matters for practitioners building privacy-preserving distributed training systems with heterogeneous, resource-constrained clients. The framework accounts for shared incentives across clients and anticipated energy consumption from both computation and networking during SFL, and it also discusses differential privacy concerns and criteria for selecting the minimum required cut layer. The analysis establishes equilibrium properties under these coupled constraints, though the work remains primarily theoretical with no reported large-scale empirical validation.

**Background**: Split Federated Learning (SFL) combines federated learning and split learning: a neural network is partitioned at a cut layer, with initial layers running on clients and the remaining layers on a training server, which reduces on-device computation while preserving data privacy. Federated learning itself faces the free-rider problem, where participants may benefit without contributing, so incentive mechanisms—often modeled with Stackelberg games—are used to encourage honest participation. DDGAD introduces a disagreement-driven method for graph anomaly detection that repurposes the Adapt-Then-Combine (ATC) framework by reversing its consensus objective: Adapt produces a node-wise estimate without same-step neighbor aggregation, while Combine forms a neighborhood-dependent contextual estimate, and their pre-consensus disagreement is accumulated across ATC steps as anomaly evidence. This work offers a fresh perspective on graph anomaly detection by treating persistent incompatibility between node-wise and contextual estimates as the anomaly signal, rather than relying solely on reconstruction error or local inconsistency mining. It could benefit researchers in graph mining and anomaly detection by providing a theoretically grounded alternative that may improve detection accuracy in domains such as fraud detection and cybersecurity. The method accumulates pre-consensus disagreement across ATC steps, and the authors derive sufficient conditions for anomaly-normal separation under contextual mixing from graph-spectral and source-response perspectives. Experiments on six benchmarks show the highest average AUROC among evaluated methods, with controlled interventions and Adapt-operator controls further supporting persistent disagreement as an effective detection signal.

The Adapt-Then-Combine (ATC) framework is a known approach in GNNs where each step first adapts node representations and then combines them with neighborhood information to reach consensus. Bioacoustic call-type classification relies on costly expert annotation, and the extreme sparsity and long-tailed distribution of target calls make it hard to spend a tight budget on the few rare, informative segments. The method addresses a temporal granularity mismatch: acquisition functions score whole segments while informative frames inside them are few, so uniform averaging washes them out. Applied frame-wise, BADGE's prediction residuals weight the aggregated pseudo-gradient, so confidently predicted no-call frames contribute little while a single uncertain rare-call frame can still set the segment's direction. Across 10 runs on a sparse, imbalanced hyena call-type dataset, BADGE-Greedy-DPP achieves the best overall and rare-call-type performance among all compared query strategies, including MFFT and the two vanilla BADGE traversals.

## [Information-Directed Sampling for Causal Bandits with Non-Manipulable Variables](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15577) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2607.15577v2) introduces causal variants of Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling (IDS) for contextual causal bandits where some variables cannot be directly manipulated but still influence rewards. The authors prove entropy-dependent sublinear Bayesian regret bounds for both methods, including a bound for IDS that explicitly accounts for Monte Carlo approximation error in expected regret and information gain. Many real-world decision problems involve variables that cannot be intervened upon but still carry information about the causal system, so extending bandit algorithms to this setting broadens their applicability. The theoretical guarantees and empirical gains over causal and non-causal baselines suggest these methods could improve sample efficiency in domains like healthcare and recommendation where interventions are limited. The work assumes a known causal graph without latent confounding and uses a Bayesian formulation where the observational conditional probability tables are the unknown parameters, letting observations under one intervention update reward estimates for others. The regret bounds depend on the action-set size in a worst-case manner, since the model contains the standard multi-armed bandit as a special case, and the paper also provides high-probability confidence bounds for the Monte Carlo estimates.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Causal bandits combine causal inference with multi-armed bandit algorithms, using knowledge of structural relationships among variables to share information across interventions and find high-reward actions faster. Information-Directed Sampling (IDS) is a decision-making principle that balances exploration and exploitation by choosing actions that minimize the ratio of expected regret to information gain, and it has previously been studied in settings such as linear partial monitoring. This paper extends both ideas to contextual causal bandits where some variables are non-manipulable.

## [Paper Formalizes the Missing-Target Problem in Generative Fairness Audits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02551) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.02551v2) formalizes the 'missing-target problem' in demographic-value-unspecified generation, where prompts like 'a CEO in the United States' leave demographic realization to the model. It decomposes target construction into four commitments—evaluative object, prior admissibility, allocation, and operationalization—and instantiates the framework in AP-Bench, finding distribution divergence from geography-derived targets ranging from 0.508 to 0.606 on a 0-to-1 scale. This work argues that target construction is not a preliminary to fairness evaluation but a component of it, meaning generative audits that compare output demographics against unjustified targets may be methodologically unsound. It affects AI fairness researchers, auditors, and policymakers who rely on demographic composition metrics to assess generative models. Replacing each geography-derived target with an equal-category comparator while holding generations and measurement fixed produces model-specific mean absolute cell-level JSD₂ changes ranging from 0.279 to 0.355. The paper admits the geographic prior under a geographic-membership interpretation for declared public-world use, but argues the occupational prior under an incumbency interpretation requires an independently defended objective such as workforce-composition fidelity.

## [VERPO converts evidence guidance into token-level credit for LLM RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06100) ⭐️ 6.0/10

VERPO introduces a verified evidence regularized policy optimization method that decomposes evidence-conditioned teacher guidance into an evidence-free reference term plus signed, evidence-induced token-level corrections, combined with a stopped controller and a Fisher Evidence Contrast (FEC) regularized projection. Across five scientific reasoning and tool-use tasks, it prevents optimization collapse and achieves the highest multi-task average across model backbones, with the largest gains on smaller models. GRPO-style methods apply a single sequence-level advantage uniformly to every token, so they cannot tell which local decisions to keep, reinforce, or revise, while evidence-conditioned self-distillation can transfer stylistic artifacts and miscalibrated confidence. VERPO's reward-aligned token-level credit assignment offers a more precise and stable training signal, which matters for researchers building reasoning and tool-use agents on top of reinforcement learning. The stopped controller performs selective acceptance, token-wise localization, and cost-aware scaling by balancing alignment with the local GRPO update direction against Fisher movement cost, while FEC attenuates nuisance shifts along an estimated evidence-presence direction. Qualitative diagnostics show token acceptance selectively targets reasoning bottlenecks consistent with local reward alignment and Fisher movement cost.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Sep 23, 04:00

**Background**: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a critic-free reinforcement learning algorithm widely used to post-train language models with verifiable rewards, but it assigns one advantage value to an entire response. Evidence-conditioned self-distillation instead uses privileged instance-level information to give denser token-level supervision, though imitating a teacher can propagate artifacts and overconfidence. VERPO sits between these two families by keeping the outcome objective while converting teacher guidance into reward-aligned, token-level credit.

A new arXiv paper (2609.06983v2) proposes a fully distributed primal-dual dynamics for quadratic generalized Nash equilibrium problems (GNEPs) that removes the need for agents to share or reach consensus on multipliers. Convergence is established under sufficient conditions using an input-to-state stability (ISS) framework, and the authors note that different initializations can lead to different GNEs, including non-variational ones. Eliminating multiplier consensus reduces inter-agent communication overhead and improves privacy, which matters for multi-agent engineering systems where sharing dual variables is costly or undesirable. The ISS-based convergence analysis also brings a mature nonlinear control tool into distributed game-theoretic optimization, potentially broadening the design and analysis toolbox for distributed algorithms. The method targets quadratic GNEPs and drops the standard requirement of multiplier consensus, so agents need not agree on dual variables; as a consequence, the equilibrium reached can depend on initialization and may be non-variational. Convergence guarantees hold only under sufficient conditions derived through the ISS framework rather than for arbitrary problem instances.

**Background**: A Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem models a game in which each player's feasible strategy set depends on the choices of other players, generalizing standard Nash equilibrium problems and arising in multi-agent engineering applications. Distributed primal-dual dynamics solve such problems by letting agents update primal (strategy) and dual (multiplier) variables over a network, and traditional schemes require the dual variables to reach consensus across agents. Input-to-state stability (ISS), introduced by Eduardo Sontag in 1989, is a nonlinear control notion characterizing how a system's state remains bounded in response to external inputs, and it is widely used to analyze interconnected and perturbed dynamical systems.
